# Optimal Loss Allocation and Reflected Free Boundaries in Systemic Risk

**Authors:** Yucheng Guo Note: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, 15213, USA, email: yuchengg@andrew.cmu.edu. Qinxin Yan Note: Industrial Engineering & Operations Research, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, 94720, USA, email: qinxinyan@berkeley.edu.

## Abstract

We study a singular mean-field control problem in which a central planner allocates losses generated by bank defaults to maximize terminal system health. Every generated loss must be borne by the surviving banks, without external capital. We prove that a cutoff, or “taxing-the-richest” rule is optimal for every non-decreasing concave terminal payoff, including the survival indicator. We construct the continuous-time optimizer by solving a time-discretized problem and passing to the limit, and establish its uniqueness in law for every non-constant payoff. The optimal flow is characterized by a novel reflected free-boundary problem. We establish well-posedness in a probabilistic solution class and prove positive-time smoothness of both the free boundary and the density of surviving banks. The main difficulty is the dependence of the limiting feedback on a moving support endpoint, which is unstable under Wasserstein convergence. We address this through stochastic-order comparisons, compactness estimates for the cutoff boundaries, and an augmented call-function formulation.

Key words: Systemic Risk, Singular Mean-Field Control, Free Boundary Problems.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 The problem and main results

The default of a financial institution can impose losses on the rest of the system and weaken institutions that remain solvent. When these losses must be borne within the system, their allocation becomes a policy question in its own right. We study a central planner who assigns losses generated by defaults among surviving banks, with the aim of preserving the system’s future health. The planner must allocate every loss in full and has no access to external capital. Our main result identifies a simple optimal rule: concentrate the burden on the currently healthiest banks. This rule is optimal for an entire class of increasing concave welfare criteria, including the proportion of banks that survive to a given horizon.

We model a representative bank by its distance to default. Before default, its state evolves as a Brownian motion minus the cumulative loss assigned to it; after default, it is absorbed at zero (and has no further role in the system). Thus, the health (net asset) of the representative bank can be described as

$$ X_{t}=X_{0}+B_{t\wedge\tau}-L_{t\wedge\tau},\quad\tau=\inf\{t\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}X_{t}=0\}, $$

where $B$ is a standard Brownian motion independent of $X_{0}$ , and $L$ is an adapted, non-decreasing allocation process that stops after default. Each default generates a loss of size $\alpha>0$ per unit of population mass to be allocated, and admissibility requires the exact aggregate balance

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t],\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

Allocation jumps may not send a solvent bank to or through zero. The allocation rule can affect future defaults and therefore the amount of loss subsequently generated. The full admissible class, allowing adapted controls on a variable probability space, is specified in Sections 2 and 3.

For a fixed horizon $T>0$ , the objective is to maximize

$$ \mathbb{E}[f(X_{T})]=\int_{[0,\infty)}f(x)\,\mu_{T}(dx),\quad\mu_{t}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t}), $$

over all admissible allocations. Here $f$ is finite, non-decreasing, and concave on $[0,\infty)$ , and may have an upward right jump at zero. In particular, $f=\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}$ gives the survival probability. We use the following standing assumption.

#### Assumption 1.1.

The initial law $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}([0,\infty))$ is compactly supported and satisfies

$$ \mu_{0}(\{0\})=0,\quad\int_{[0,\infty)}x\,\mu_{0}(dx)>\alpha. $$

No density or boundary compatibility condition is imposed on $\mu_{0}$ . The strict mean condition ensures a positive reserve margin: exact loss balance gives $\mathbb{E}[X_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]>0$ .

#### Optimal loss allocation.

We first separate Brownian evolution from allocation on a time grid. At each allocation date, all banks above an endogenous cutoff are reduced to that cutoff, while banks below it are left unchanged. The cutoff is chosen to match exactly the losses generated since the preceding allocation date. Proposition 2.3 identifies this rule as the one-step maximizer in increasing-concave order, and Theorem 2.7 establishes its dynamic optimality. The same cutoff rule therefore optimizes every payoff in the stated class.

As the time step tends to zero, the discrete values converge to the continuous-time value, and the discrete optimal controls yield an admissible optimal limit (Theorem 3.1). In this limit, the cutoff becomes a deterministic moving upper boundary $\Lambda$ : surviving banks are reflected downward at $\Lambda$ and absorbed at zero. The resulting control is optimal in the full admissible class. Moreover, for every nonconstant payoff $f$ , both the optimal law flow and the joint law of the optimal state and allocation process are unique (Theorem 5.4). This uniqueness includes the survival payoff and does not require strict concavity.

#### A well-posed and smooth free boundary.

The optimal dynamics lead to a novel parabolic free-boundary problem. For positive times, let $u(t,\cdot)$ denote the density of the surviving population, whose total mass is $\mathbb{P}[\tau>t]$ . The density and the upper boundary satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{t}u(t,x) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}u(t,x), \displaystyle 0<x<\Lambda_{t}, \displaystyle u(t,0) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x}u(t,\Lambda_{t}) \displaystyle=-\dot{\Lambda}_{t}u(t,\Lambda_{t}), \displaystyle u(t,\Lambda_{t}) \displaystyle=\alpha\partial_{x}u(t,0). $$

The first two boundary conditions describe absorption at zero and reflection at the moving upper edge. The last condition couples the two ends of the interval: the allocation at the reflecting boundary must fund the losses generated by the default flux at the origin.

We first establish well-posedness in a probabilistic solution class that does not assume a smooth boundary. The construction in Section 3 provides existence, and an augmented call-function formulation yields stability and uniqueness (Theorem 4.20 and Corollary 4.21). We then prove that $\Lambda$ is actually smooth at every positive time and that $u$ is smooth up to both spatial boundaries, so that (1.1) holds classically (Theorem 4.25 and Remark 4.26). Therefore, classical free-boundary dynamics emerge even from singular initial laws. The stability estimates also give Lipschitz continuity of the value function in a distance that records initial call functions and absorption probabilities under uncontrolled Brownian evolution (Proposition 5.1).

The main analytical difficulty appears as the allocation time step vanishes: the loss budgets become small, and the cutoffs approach a support endpoint, which is not controlled by ordinary Wasserstein convergence. We combine stochastic-order comparisons with compactness estimates for the cutoff boundaries to construct the optimal limit. The augmented call function then encodes both the distribution of surviving reserves and the accumulated defaults, making it possible to prove uniqueness before establishing boundary regularity.

#### Organization of the paper.

In the remainder of this section, we briefly discuss the connection of our model to the literature. Section 2 solves the discrete-time control problem. Section 3 constructs an optimal continuous-time control by passage to the limit. Section 4 establishes well-posedness and positive-time classical regularity of the associated free boundary. Section 5 proves stability of the value function and uniqueness of the optimal control. Auxiliary stochastic-order results are collected in the Appendix Section A.

### 1.2 Related literature

#### Systemic risk and loss allocation.

Financial-network models describe how contractual obligations transmit distress, beginning with the clearing framework of Eisenberg and Noe [14]. Dynamic interbank models also connect reserve fluctuations and lending decisions to systemic risk; see, for example, the mean-field game of Carmona, Fouque, and Sun [9]. Particularly close to our setting are absorbed mean-field models in which defaults impose losses on surviving institutions. Hambly, Ledger, and Søjmark [19] analyze the resulting positive feedback and blow-ups, while common noise and heterogeneous contagion are studied in [20, 15]. These models make the dependence of future defaults on the transmission of current losses explicit.

Centralized intervention in contagious default systems has been studied through capital injections by Cuchiero, Reisinger, and Rigger [11] and Hambly and Jettkant [18]. Survival-oriented budget allocation is considered by Bayraktar, Guo, Tang, and Zhang [2]. Our planner instead chooses how to distribute the losses generated within the system. Each realized loss must be funded by the surviving population, and its distribution influences subsequent defaults. This isolates the allocation of endogenous losses as a control problem and identifies a rule that maximizes an entire class of terminal welfare measures.

#### Mean-field control and games.

Our problem belongs to centralized control of McKean–Vlasov dynamics: the planner optimizes the population’s welfare while accounting for the effect of intervention on its law. The distinction from mean-field games is developed by Carmona, Delarue, and Lachapelle [8]; dynamic programming on the space of probability measures is established, among other works, by Pham and Wei [23]. Singular interventions have been studied in mean-field games by Fu and Horst [17], in mean-field control with multidimensional singular controls by Denkert and Horst [13], and under dynamic state-control-law constraints by Bo, Wang, and Yu [5]. Endogenous reflection boundaries also arise in the interbank singular-control games of Cont, Guo, and Xu [10].

The specific difficulty here comes from combining absorption with an exact balance between cumulative intervention and default mass. The default mass and the optimal support boundary are unstable under ordinary Wasserstein convergence. General existence or dynamic-programming results do not by themselves identify the cutoff optimizer or determine its free boundary. Our approach uses the order structure of the allocation problem to solve the discrete dynamics and then analyze the singular limit. It also identifies the same unique optimal control for every nonconstant payoff in the prescribed class.

#### Parabolic free-boundary problems.

The connection between singular mean-field interactions and Stefan problems is central to the probabilistic analysis of default contagion. Delarue, Nadtochiy, and Shkolnikov [12] establish global physical solutions, regularity, and uniqueness for the supercooled Stefan problem in the presence of blow-ups. The bailout model of [11] leads to a drift-controlled version of that problem. In our system, absorption occurs at a fixed endpoint and the moving endpoint is reflecting. The boundary condition $u(t,\Lambda_{t})=\alpha\partial_{x}u(t,0)$ couples the reflecting density to the default flux at the opposite endpoint. Reflection in prescribed time-dependent intervals is studied by Burdzy, Kang, and Ramanan [6]; here in this paper, the boundary must itself be determined consistently with this coupling. The probabilistic and augmented call-function formulations allow us to establish well-posedness under Assumption 1.1 and subsequently recover smooth classical solutions at positive times.

#### Particle systems with selection.

Extremal intervention also produces free boundaries in diffusing particle systems with selection. Carinci, De Masi, Giardinà, and Presutti [7] construct generalized free-boundary solutions through mass-transport inequalities and barriers obtained by alternating diffusion with removal and reinjection. Berestycki, Brunet, Nolen, and Penington [3] study the free-boundary problem associated with branching Brownian motion with spatial selection. Atar [1] develops a weak formulation in terms of a density and a selection measure, encoding extremal removal without assuming a regular interface. These works provide close precedents for the use of order, splitting approximations, and weak formulations to analyze moving support boundaries. Our cutoff transports the upper tail to a threshold while retaining its surviving mass, and the amount allocated is determined by defaults at the origin. Its limiting boundary therefore reflects surviving states and has a positive density trace. The approximation studied here is the vanishing allocation-time step.

#### Stochastic order and optimal allocation.

The cutoff argument is also related to majorization and stochastic dominance; see Shaked and Shanthikumar [24]. For a fixed loss budget, capping the largest reserves produces the maximal feasible law in increasing-concave order. The dynamic issue is that the allocation changes future defaults and hence future budgets. The comparisons in Sections 2 and 3 preserve the relevant order through this feedback, extending a static allocation principle to the full control problem.

## 2 Discrete-Time Cutoff Control

In this section, we study the time-discretized version of the mean-field control problem. Let the time step $\Delta>0$ be such that $M\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=T/\Delta$ is an integer, and write $t_{n}=n\Delta$ . With the aim to de-couple the Brownian evolution of individual banks and the allocation control, we assume that the Brownian motion and the default (absorption at $0$ ) still evolves in continuous time, while losses generated by defaults during $(t_{n},t_{n+1}]$ are deferred to and allocated at $t_{n+1}$ .

### 2.1 Admissible controls and the law-valued state

We first give a process-level formulation. An admissible system is defined on a filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{0\leq t\leq T},\mathbb{P})$ satisfying the usual conditions. It carries an $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ -measurable initial state $X_{0}$ with $\mathcal{L}(X_{0})=\mu_{0}$ and an $(\mathcal{F}_{t})$ -Brownian motion $B$ independent of $X_{0}$ . The space may also carry independent auxiliary random variables, independent of $(X_{0},B)$ and revealed only at allocation dates. These variables allow for relaxed, randomized allocation kernels. It turns out that, as we will see in Section 2.3, the cutoff optimizer constructed below does not use this randomization.

Suppose that $X_{t_{n}}$ is the post-allocation state at time $t_{n}$ . On $[t_{n},t_{n+1})$ , let

$$ \widehat{\tau}_{n+1}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\left\{t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}X_{t_{n}}+B_{t}-B_{t_{n}}\leq 0\right\}, $$

with the convention that $\inf\varnothing=\infty$ , and set

$$ X_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\begin{cases}X_{t_{n}}+B_{t}-B_{t_{n}},&t<\widehat{\tau}_{n+1},\\
0,&t\geq\widehat{\tau}_{n+1},\end{cases}\qquad t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}), $$

and

$$ \widehat{X}_{t_{n+1}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{t_{n+1}-}=\begin{cases}X_{t_{n}}+B_{t_{n+1}}-B_{t_{n}},&\widehat{\tau}_{n+1}>t_{n+1},\\
0,&\widehat{\tau}_{n+1}\leq t_{n+1}.\end{cases} $$

An allocation $A_{n+1}$ is an $\mathcal{F}_{t_{n+1}}$ -measurable random variable and satisfies

$$ A_{n+1}=0\ \text{on }\{\widehat{X}_{t_{n+1}}=0\},\quad 0\leq A_{n+1}<\widehat{X}_{t_{n+1}}\ \text{on }\{\widehat{\tau}_{n+1}>t_{n+1}\}. $$

The post-allocation state is

$$ X_{t_{n+1}}=\widehat{X}_{t_{n+1}}-A_{n+1}. $$

After a bank defaults, it remains at zero and receives no later allocation. With

$$ L_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sum_{k=1}^{M}A_{k}\mathbf{1}_{\{t_{k}\leq t\}}, $$

the cumulative allocated loss is thus adapted, nonnegative, non-decreasing, càdlàg, integrable, and satisfies $L_{t}=L_{t\wedge\tau}$ , where

$$ \tau\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}X_{t}=0\}. $$

The aggregate-loss constraint is imposed as an equality at allocation dates:

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t_{n}}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t_{n}],\qquad n=0,\ldots,M. $$

Defaults occurring between two grid times are therefore outstanding until the next allocation date. At $t_{0}=0$ , the standing assumption $\mu_{0}(\{0\})=0$ and the convention $L_{0}=0$ make (2.2) automatic. Thus $\mu_{0}$ is already the post-allocation law at the initial date.

This is a weak/open-loop admissible class: the probability space is part of the control, and allocations may use the information in $\mathcal{F}_{t_{n}}$ . Because future Brownian increments are independent of $\mathcal{F}_{t_{n}}$ and the objective depends only on the terminal law, every one-step open-loop allocation can be represented by its conditional allocation kernel given the current pre-allocation state. Conversely, every such Borel kernel can be realized using the auxiliary randomization. Thus, there is no loss in using relaxed Markov law-feedback controls for the Bellman recursion below.

Let $\mu_{n}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t_{n}})$ and let $\widehat{\mu}_{n+1}=S_{\Delta}\mu_{n}$ be the pre-allocation law, where $S_{t}$ is the absorbed Brownian semigroup defined below. If $q_{\mu}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu(\{0\})$ denotes the mass of $\mu$ at $x=0$ , then (2.2) is equivalent to

$$ \mathbb{E}[A_{n+1}]=c_{\Delta}(\mu_{n})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\alpha\bigl(q_{S_{\Delta}\mu_{n}}-q_{\mu_{n}}\bigr). $$

For a continuation problem restarted at $t_{n}$ from a post-allocation law $\mu$ , the atom $q_{\mu}$ records defaults whose losses have already been funded. The future allocations therefore satisfy the shifted balance

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=n+1}^{j}A_{k}\right]=\alpha\bigl(q_{\mu_{j}}-q_{\mu}\bigr),\quad j=n+1,\ldots,M, $$

where $\mu_{j}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t_{j}})$ . This is the continuation convention used in the Bellman recursion. For $n=0$ , $\mu=\mu_{0}$ , and $q_{\mu_{0}}=0$ , it coincides with (2.2).

### 2.2 Stochastic orders and the cutoff operator

Throughout the paper,

$$ \mathbb{R}_{+}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=[0,\infty),\quad\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}_{+})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x)<\infty\right\}. $$

We write $\Phi_{\mathrm{G}}$ and $\varphi_{\mathrm{G}}$ for the standard Gaussian CDF and density, and $\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=1-\Phi_{\mathrm{G}}$ for its upper tail. For $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ , we define the following objects, the meaning of which will become evident as we proceed with the analysis:

$$ \displaystyle m_{\mu} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x), \displaystyle q_{\mu} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu(\{0\}), \displaystyle h_{\mu} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\alpha q_{\mu}, \displaystyle C_{\mu}(a) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(x-a)^{+}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x), \displaystyle D_{\mu}(a) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(x\wedge a)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x), \displaystyle H_{\mu}(a) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=C_{\mu}(a)+h_{\mu}. $$

Note that $D_{\mu}(a)=m_{\mu}-C_{\mu}(a)$ .

#### Definition 2.1.

For $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ :

- 1. $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ denotes first-order stochastic dominance:

$$ \int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu\geq\int f\,\mathrm{d}\nu $$

for every non-decreasing Borel function $f$ of at most linear growth.

- 2. $\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ denotes second-order stochastic dominance:

$$ \int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu\geq\int f\,\mathrm{d}\nu $$

for every finite non-decreasing concave function $f\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ of at most linear growth.

#### Remark 2.2.

We briefly comment on the set of testing functions $f$ in item 2 of Definition 2.1. By allowing a possible upward jump at $x=0$ , we include the survival payoff function $\mathbf{1}_{\{x>0\}}$ . Indeed, every such $f$ has the decomposition

$$ f(x)=f(0)+J_{f}\mathbf{1}_{\{x>0\}}+\int_{0}^{x}g(s)\,\mathrm{d}s,\quad J_{f}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=f(0+)-f(0)\geq 0, $$

where $g$ is non-negative and non-increasing. Equivalently, for a right-continuous version of $g$ , there are $\ell\geq 0$ and a positive Stieltjes measure $\gamma$ such that

$$ f(x)=f(0)+J_{f}\mathbf{1}_{\{x>0\}}+\ell x+\int_{(0,\infty)}(x\wedge a)\,\gamma(\mathrm{d}a). $$

It follows that

$$ \mu\succsim_{2}\nu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_{\mu}(a)\geq D_{\nu}(a)\quad\text{for every }a>0. $$

The survival term can be recovered from

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\{x>0\}}=\lim_{a\downarrow 0}\frac{x\wedge a}{a}. $$

In particular, $f=\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}$ corresponds to $J_{f}=1$ and $g=0$ .

For $0\leq c<m_{\mu}$ , define the exact-budget action set

$$ \mathcal{A}(\mu,c)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\{\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mu\succsim_{1}\nu,\quad q_{\nu}=q_{\mu},\quad m_{\nu}=m_{\mu}-c\right\}. $$

The equality of the atoms at zero is the law-level form of the no-allocation-induced-default condition.

The cutoff operator has the following precise domain. Set $T_{0}\mu=\mu$ . If $0<c<m_{\mu}$ , the call function is continuous and strictly decreasing while positive, so there is a unique $\kappa_{c}(\mu)>0$ such that

$$ C_{\mu}(\kappa_{c}(\mu))=c. $$

Define

$$ T_{c}\mu\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\bigl(x\mapsto x\wedge\kappa_{c}(\mu)\bigr)_{\#}\mu. $$

We leave $T_{c}\mu$ undefined for $c\geq m_{\mu}$ .

#### Proposition 2.3 (Cutoff maximality).

Let $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ and $0\leq c<m_{\mu}$ . Then $T_{c}\mu\in\mathcal{A}(\mu,c)$ . Moreover, $T_{c}\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ for every $\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ satisfying $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ and $m_{\nu}\leq m_{\mu}-c$ .

#### Proof.

The case $c=0$ is trivial. Suppose henceforth that $0<c<m_{\mu}$ . Under the pointwise coupling $X\mapsto X\wedge\kappa_{c}(\mu)$ , the pre-allocation state is at least the post-allocation state, so it is clear that $\mu\succsim_{1}T_{c}\mu$ . It lowers the mean by $C_{\mu}(\kappa_{c}(\mu))=c$ , hence belongs to $\mathcal{A}(\mu,c)$ . For every $a\geq 0$ ,

$$ C_{T_{c}\mu}(a)=\bigl(C_{\mu}(a)-c\bigr)^{+}, $$

and therefore

$$ D_{T_{c}\mu}(a)=\min\{D_{\mu}(a),m_{\mu}-c\}. $$

If $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ , then the increasing function $x\mapsto x\wedge a$ gives $D_{\mu}(a)\geq D_{\nu}(a)$ . Also $D_{\nu}(a)\leq m_{\nu}\leq m_{\mu}-c$ . Hence,

$$ D_{T_{c}\mu}(a)\geq D_{\nu}(a)\quad\forall a>0. $$

The characterization (2.8) proves the result. ∎

For $t\geq 0$ , let $S_{t}\mu$ be the law at time $t$ of Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ absorbed on hitting zero, with initial law $\mu$ . Equivalently,

$$ S_{t}\mu(\mathrm{d}x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int\mathbb{P}\Big[y+B_{t}\in\mathrm{d}x,\inf_{s\in[0,t]}(y+B_{s})>0\Big]\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)+\int\mathbb{P}\Big[\inf_{s\in[0,t]}(y+B_{s})\leq 0\Big]\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\cdot\delta_{0}(\mathrm{d}x). $$

#### Lemma 2.4 (Order preservation).

Let $t>0$ .

- 1. If $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ , then $S_{t}\mu\succsim_{1}S_{t}\nu$ .

- 2. If $\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ , then $S_{t}\mu\succsim_{2}S_{t}\nu$ .

- 3. If $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ and $0\leq c<\min\{m_{\mu},m_{\nu}\}$ , then $T_{c}\mu\succsim_{1}T_{c}\nu$ .

- 4. If $\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ and $0\leq c<\min\{m_{\mu},m_{\nu}\}$ , then $T_{c}\mu\succsim_{2}T_{c}\nu$ .

#### Proof.

Absorbed semigroup and first-order dominance. If $x\geq y$ , we couple the two Brownian trajectories $B^{x}$ , $B^{y}$ with absorption at $0$ starting from $x$ and $y$ . Before the smaller process is absorbed, their difference is $x-y$ , and after that time the smaller process is zero. Thus, $B_{t}^{x}\geq B_{t}^{y}$ for every $t$ . Applying the monotone coupling characterization of first-order dominance proves the first claim.

Absorbed semigroup and second-order dominance. Let $S_{t}f(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{E}[f(B_{t}^{x})]$ . The preceding coupling shows that $S_{t}f$ is non-decreasing when $f$ is non-decreasing. It remains to prove concavity for the basis in (2.7). Optional stopping gives $S_{t}\mathrm{id}(x)=x$ . For the endpoint jump,

$$ S_{t}\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}(x)=2\Phi_{\mathrm{G}}\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{t}}\right)-1,\quad x>0, $$

with value zero at $x=0$ . Its second derivative is

$$ -\frac{2x}{t^{3/2}}\varphi_{\mathrm{G}}\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\leq 0,\quad\forall x>0. $$

The density of Brownian motion absorbed at $0$ is

$$ p_{t}^{0}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\left(e^{-(x-y)^{2}/(2t)}-e^{-(x+y)^{2}/(2t)}\right),\quad x,y>0. $$

For $a>0$ , set

$$ v_{a}(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=S_{t}\bigl((\,\cdot-a)^{+}\bigr)(x)=\int_{a}^{\infty}(y-a)p_{t}^{0}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}y. $$

Since $\partial_{xx}p_{t}^{0}=\partial_{yy}p_{t}^{0}$ , integrating-by-part twice gives

$$ \partial_{xx}v_{a}(t,x)=p_{t}^{0}(x,a)\geq 0. $$

As $S_{t}(x\wedge a)=x-v_{a}(t,x)$ , this function is concave; it is non-decreasing by the pathwise coupling. The positive mixture (2.7) now shows that $S_{t}f$ is non-decreasing and concave. Therefore

$$ \int f\,\mathrm{d}(S_{t}\mu)=\int S_{t}f\,\mathrm{d}\mu\geq\int S_{t}f\,\mathrm{d}\nu=\int f\,\mathrm{d}(S_{t}\nu), $$

which proves the second claim.

Cutoff operator and first-order dominance. If $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ , then $C_{\mu}(a)\geq C_{\nu}(a)$ for every $a$ . Hence $\kappa_{c}(\mu)\geq\kappa_{c}(\nu)$ . Couple $X\sim\mu$ and $Y\sim\nu$ so that $X\geq Y$ almost surely. Then

$$ X\wedge\kappa_{c}(\mu)\geq Y\wedge\kappa_{c}(\nu)\quad\text{almost surely}, $$

which proves the third claim.

Cutoff operator and second-order dominance. First, we suppose that $m_{\mu}=m_{\nu}$ . Then $\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ is equivalent to $C_{\mu}(a)\leq C_{\nu}(a)$ for every $a$ . Identity (2.12) gives

$$ C_{T_{c}\mu}(a)\leq C_{T_{c}\nu}(a), $$

and the two post-tax means are equal, so $T_{c}\mu\succsim_{2}T_{c}\nu$ .

For unequal means, we apply Lemma A.1: there is $\eta\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ such that $\eta\succsim_{1}\nu$ and that $\eta$ dominates $\mu$ in convex order. Equivalently, $m_{\eta}=m_{\mu}$ and $\mu\succsim_{2}\eta$ . The equal-mean case and the third claim yield

$$ T_{c}\mu\succsim_{2}T_{c}\eta\succsim_{1}T_{c}\nu, $$

which proves the last claim. ∎

#### Lemma 2.5 (Correct coupling direction for an allocation).

Let $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ and $0\leq c<m_{\mu}$ . Then $\nu\in\mathcal{A}(\mu,c)$ if and only if there is a coupling $(X,Y)$ such that

$$ X\sim\mu,\quad Y\sim\nu,\quad X\geq Y\ \text{almost surely},\quad\mathbb{E}[X-Y]=c, $$

and $X=0$ if and only if $Y=0$ almost surely. Thus, $X$ is the pre-allocation state and the dominated variable $Y$ is the post-allocation state. The allocated loss $A=X-Y$ satisfies

$$ A=0\ \text{on }\{X=0\},\quad 0\leq A<X\ \text{on }\{X>0\}. $$

#### Proof.

If $\nu\in\mathcal{A}(\mu,c)$ , the monotone quantile coupling gives $X\geq Y$ almost surely. Since $q_{\mu}=q_{\nu}$ , $Y=0$ must almost surely imply $X=0$ , so $X=0$ if and only if $Y=0$ . The mean identity gives $\mathbb{E}[X-Y]=c$ . The strict inequality $X-Y<X$ on $\{X>0\}$ follows from $Y>0$ there. Conversely, the stated coupling implies $\mu\succsim_{1}\nu$ , equality of the atoms at zero, and $m_{\nu}=m_{\mu}-c$ .

∎

### 2.3 Bellman recursion and optimality

For clarifying the comparison analyzed in this section, we define the total-resource functional and the order

$$ \mathcal{R}(\mu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{\mu}+\alpha q_{\mu}=H_{\mu}(0),\qquad\mu\succsim_{\alpha}\nu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu\succsim_{2}\nu\ \text{and}\,\,\mathcal{R}(\mu)\geq\mathcal{R}(\nu). $$

For a general $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ (treated as a post-allocation distribution), set

$$ c_{\Delta}(\mu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\alpha(q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}-q_{\mu}),\quad\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=T_{c_{\Delta}(\mu)}S_{\Delta}\mu. $$

#### Lemma 2.6 (Exact-balance invariant and one-step order).

If $\mathcal{R}(\mu)>\alpha$ , then $0<c_{\Delta}(\mu)<m_{\mu}=m_{S_{\Delta}\mu}$ , so $\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)$ is an admissible strict-domain cutoff update. It satisfies

$$ q_{\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)}=q_{S_{\Delta}\mu},\quad\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu))=\mathcal{R}(\mu). $$

Every distribution in $\mathcal{A}(S_{\Delta}\mu,c_{\Delta}(\mu))$ has the same value of $\mathcal{R}$ . Moreover, if both $\mathcal{R}(\mu)>\alpha$ and $\mathcal{R}(\nu)>\alpha$ , then

$$ \mu\succsim_{\alpha}\nu\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\succsim_{\alpha}\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\nu). $$

#### Proof.

Absorbed Brownian motion preserves the mean by optional stopping. Note also that $\mathcal{R}(\mu)>\alpha$ implies $q_{\mu}<1$ . From every $x>0$ , Brownian motion starting at $x$ has strictly positive probability of hitting zero before time $\Delta$ , so $q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}>q_{\mu}$ and $c_{\Delta}(\mu)>0$ . Since also $q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}\leq 1$ ,

$$ m_{\mu}-c_{\Delta}(\mu)=m_{\mu}+\alpha q_{\mu}-\alpha q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}=\mathcal{R}(\mu)-\alpha q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}\geq\mathcal{R}(\mu)-\alpha>0. $$

Thus, the cutoff is in the strict domain and preserves the atom at zero. Exact balance gives the asserted resource identity. The same calculation applies to every distribution in the action set $\mathcal{A}(S_{\Delta}\mu,c_{\Delta}(\mu))$ .

Now suppose $\mathcal{R}(\nu)>\alpha$ and $\mu\succsim_{\alpha}\nu$ . Lemma 2.4 gives

$$ S_{\Delta}\mu\succsim_{2}S_{\Delta}\nu,\quad q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}\leq q_{S_{\Delta}\nu}, $$

where the second inequality uses the survival payoff $\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}$ . By (2.13),

$$ D_{\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)}(a)=\min\left\{D_{S_{\Delta}\mu}(a),\mathcal{R}(\mu)-\alpha q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}\right\}. $$

Both entries in this minimum dominate the corresponding entries for $\nu$ . Hence

$$ D_{\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)}(a)\geq D_{\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\nu)}(a)\quad\text{for all }a>0. $$

The characterization (2.8) and resource invariance prove the claim. ∎

Let $f$ be a finite non-decreasing concave payoff of at most linear growth, with the endpoint convention in Definition 2.1. For post-allocation laws with $\mathcal{R}(\mu)>\alpha$ , we recursively define the value functions

$$ \displaystyle V_{f}^{\Delta}(T,\mu) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}f(x)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x), \displaystyle V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n},\mu) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{\rho\in\mathcal{A}(S_{\Delta}\mu,c_{\Delta}(\mu))}V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n+1},\rho),\quad n=M-1,\ldots,0. $$

This is the Bellman recursion for the shifted weak/open-loop continuation problem (2.4), after Markovization by conditional allocation kernels.

#### Theorem 2.7 (Discrete cutoff optimality).

On the domain

$$ \mathfrak{D}_{\alpha}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathcal{R}(\mu)>\alpha\}, $$

the following assertions hold for every $n=0,\ldots,M$ :

- 1. $V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n},\cdot)$ is non-decreasing with respect to $\succsim_{\alpha}$ ;

- 2. the supremum in (2.16) is attained and

$$ V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n},\mu)=V_{f}^{\Delta}\bigl(t_{n+1},\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\bigr),\quad n<M; $$

- 3. the deterministic cutoff law-feedback policy

$$ \mu_{n+1}=\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu_{n}) $$

is an optimizer for the shifted continuation problem. In particular, it is an optimizer for the original problem started from $\mu_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

We use backward induction and prove the first two assertions simultaneously. At $n=M$ , monotonicity follows from the definition of $\succsim_{2}$ .

Assume that $V_{f,n+1}^{\Delta}$ is non-decreasing for $\succsim_{\alpha}$ . If $\rho\in\mathcal{A}(S_{\Delta}\mu,c_{\Delta}(\mu))$ , then Proposition 2.3 gives $\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\succsim_{2}\rho$ . The two laws have the same mean and the same atom at zero, hence the same resource $\mathcal{R}$ . Therefore, $\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\succsim_{\alpha}\rho$ , and the induction hypothesis gives

$$ V_{f}^{\Delta}\bigl(t_{n+1},\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\bigr)\geq V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n+1},\rho). $$

Since the cutoff law itself belongs to the action set, it attains the Bellman supremum. If $\mu,\nu\in\mathfrak{D}_{\alpha}$ and $\mu\succsim_{\alpha}\nu$ , Lemma 2.6 and the induction hypothesis yield

$$ \displaystyle V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n},\mu)=V_{f}^{\Delta}\bigl(t_{n+1},\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu)\bigr)\geq V_{f}^{\Delta}\bigl(t_{n+1},\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\nu)\bigr)=V_{f}^{\Delta}(t_{n},\nu). $$

This closes the induction.

Finally, on the strict domain $\mathfrak{D}_{\alpha}$ ,

$$ \kappa_{c}(\mu)=\inf\{a\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}C_{\mu}(a)\leq c\}. $$

The map $(\mu,a)\mapsto C_{\mu}(a)$ is continuous under the $W_{1}$ topology in $\mu$ and the usual topology in $a$ , so the displayed formula makes $(\mu,c)\mapsto\kappa_{c}(\mu)$ Borel on the positive strict domain. Moreover, $\mu\mapsto S_{\Delta}\mu$ is $W_{1}$ -continuous, $\mu\mapsto q_{\mu}$ is Borel, and

$$ q_{S_{\Delta}\mu}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq\Delta}(x+B_{s})\leq 0\right]\mu(\mathrm{d}x) $$

is continuous because the hitting-probability kernel is bounded and continuous. Hence, $c_{\Delta}$ , $\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}$ , and $(x,\mu)\mapsto(x-\kappa_{c_{\Delta}(\mu)}(S_{\Delta}\mu))^{+}$ are Borel. The positivity established in Lemma 2.6 ensures that the positive-cutoff formula applies throughout $\mathfrak{D}_{\alpha}$ . Iterating this selector realizes the cutoff law sequence and proves the genuine optimizer statement.

∎

## 3 Continuous-Time Optimality via Time Discretization

### 3.1 Continuous-time controls and the main result

The continuous model uses the same exact aggregate-loss balance as the discrete model. We first define the process-level formulation of the weak/open-loop control problem. The compactness and identification needed to connect it to the discrete cutoff systems are addressed separately.

Fix a law $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ . As in the discrete case in Section 2, an admissible system is defined on a filtered probability space $\bigl(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{0\leq t\leq T},\mathbb{P}\bigr)$ satisfying the usual conditions. It carries an $\mathcal{F}_{0}$ -measurable initial state $X_{0}$ with $\mathcal{L}(X_{0})=\mu_{0}$ and an $(\mathcal{F}_{t})$ -Brownian motion $B$ independent of $X_{0}$ . The space may also carry independent auxiliary random variables, independent of $(X_{0},B)$ , allowing potential randomness on the allocation control.

The cumulative allocation $L$ is $(\mathcal{F}_{t})$ -adapted, non-negative, non-decreasing, càdlàg, and satisfies

$$ L_{0-}=L_{0}=0,\quad\mathbb{E}[L_{T}]<\infty. $$

Define the unabsorbed reserve and default time by

$$ \widehat{X}_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t}-L_{t},\quad\tau\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\big\{t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\widehat{X}_{t}\leq 0\big\}, $$

with $\inf\varnothing=\infty$ . The allocation is required to stop at default:

$$ L_{t}=L_{t\wedge\tau},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

Allocation jumps may not default a surviving bank: almost surely, for every $t\in[0,T]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta L_{t} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\text{on }\{t\leq\tau,\ \widehat{X}_{t-}=0\}, \displaystyle 0\leq\Delta L_{t} \displaystyle<\widehat{X}_{t-}, \displaystyle\text{on }\{t\leq\tau,\ \widehat{X}_{t-}>0\}. $$

Here, the no-allocation-induced-default convention means precisely that an allocation jump cannot send a positive reserve to or through zero. Since Brownian paths are continuous and every downward jump of $\widehat{X}$ equals $-\Delta L$ , condition (3.4) implies $\widehat{X}_{\tau}=0$ on $\{\tau\leq T\}$ .

The absorbed state is

$$ X_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\begin{cases}\widehat{X}_{t},&t<\tau,\\
0,&t\geq\tau.\end{cases} $$

Equivalently,

$$ X_{t}=X_{0}+B_{t\wedge\tau}-L_{t\wedge\tau},\quad t\in[0,T], $$

so the process remains at zero after default. We also note that $\tau$ also equals the first zero-hitting time of $X$ .

The aggregate relation is imposed again as the exact balance

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t],\quad\forall t\in[0,T]. $$

In particular, the convention $L_{0-}=0$ and exact balance force $L_{0}=0$ in the original problem.

This is a weak/open-loop class: the filtered probability space is part of the control, and $L$ need not be Markov or law-feedback. Exact balance makes the current law sufficient for the resource bookkeeping. Indeed, if $\mu_{t}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t})$ , then optional stopping in (3.6) gives

$$ m_{\mu_{t}}+\alpha q_{\mu_{t}}=m_{\mu_{0}}+\alpha q_{\mu_{0}},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

Let $\mathfrak{A}(\mu_{0})$ denote the class of admissible system $(X,B,L,\tau)$ above. For a payoff $f$ as in item 2 of Definition 2.1, define

$$ V_{f}(0,\mu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{\mathfrak{A}(\mu)}\mathbb{E}[f(X_{T})]. $$

For the survival payoff, retain the abbreviation

$$ V(0,\mu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=V_{\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}}(0,\mu). $$

We can also restart the control problem at some time $r\in[0,T]$ as in Section 2.

#### Theorem 3.1.

Suppose that Assumption 1.1 holds. Then

$$ \displaystyle V_{f}(0,\mu_{0})=\lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0}V_{f}^{\Delta}(0,\mu_{0}) $$

for any payoff function $f$ as in item 2 of Definition 2.1.

The proof has two parts. First, we compare the discrete cutoff flow with an arbitrary continuous-time admissible control and obtain $V_{f}^{\Delta}\geq V_{f}$ ; this part is easier as, intuitively, delaying the default loss benefits the overall health of the system. For the reverse inequality, we realize the discrete cutoff flow by stopped reflection, establish positive-time compactness of the associated boundaries, and identify every subsequential limit as an admissible optimal continuous-time control.

### 3.2 Discrete cutoff controls dominate continuous-time competitors

Fix an arbitrary admissible continuous-time system $(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{B},\widetilde{L},\widetilde{\tau})\in\mathfrak{A}(\mu_{0})$ , and write $t_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=n\Delta$ , $\widetilde{\mu}_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{X}_{t})$ . The exact shifted balance and the stopped state equation imply the resource identity

$$ R(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})=m_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}+\alpha q_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}=R(\mu_{0})=\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}R_{0},\quad n=0,\ldots,M. $$

#### Lemma 3.2.

The following one-step comparison holds:

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})\succsim_{\alpha}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}},\quad n=0,\ldots,M-1. $$

#### Proof.

Fix $n$ , and, on the same probability space, switch off all allocation after $t_{n}$ . More precisely, define

$$ \widehat{\tau}_{n+1}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\left\{s\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\widetilde{X}_{t_{n}}+\widetilde{B}_{s}-\widetilde{B}_{t_{n}}\leq 0\right\}, $$

with the convention $\inf\varnothing=\infty$ , and set

$$ \widehat{X}_{n+1}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\bigl(\widetilde{X}_{t_{n}}+\widetilde{B}_{t_{n+1}}-\widetilde{B}_{t_{n}}\bigr)\mathbf{1}_{\{\widehat{\tau}_{n+1}>t_{n+1}\}}. $$

Because $\widetilde{X}_{t_{n}}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{t_{n}}$ -measurable and the future Brownian increments are independent of $\mathcal{F}_{t_{n}}$ , we see that $\mathcal{L}(\widehat{X}_{n+1})=S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}$ . We claim that

$$ \widehat{X}_{n+1}\geq\widetilde{X}_{t_{n+1}}\quad\text{almost surely}. $$

Indeed, on $\{\widetilde{\tau}\leq t_{n+1}\}$ , the right-hand side is zero, so the claim is immediate. On $\{\widetilde{\tau}>t_{n+1}\}$ , for every $s\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}]$ ,

$$ \widetilde{X}_{s}=\widetilde{X}_{t_{n}}+\widetilde{B}_{s}-\widetilde{B}_{t_{n}}-\bigl(\widetilde{L}_{s}-\widetilde{L}_{t_{n}}\bigr)>0. $$

Since $\widetilde{L}_{s}-\widetilde{L}_{t_{n}}\geq 0$ , the path $\widetilde{X}_{t_{n}}+\widetilde{B}_{s}-\widetilde{B}_{t_{n}}$ also remains positive throughout the interval. Thus, $\widehat{\tau}_{n+1}>t_{n+1}$ , and

$$ \widehat{X}_{n+1}=\widetilde{X}_{t_{n+1}}+\widetilde{L}_{t_{n+1}}-\widetilde{L}_{t_{n}}\geq\widetilde{X}_{t_{n+1}}. $$

This proves (3.12), and consequently

$$ S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}\succsim_{1}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}. $$

In particular, applying this dominance to $\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}$ gives

$$ q_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}\leq q_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}}. $$

Let

$$ c_{n+1}^{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=c_{\Delta}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})=\alpha\bigl(q_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}-q_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}\bigr)\geq 0 $$

be the genuine discrete-time budget associated with $\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}$ . Absorbed Brownian motion preserves the first moment, so $m_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}=m_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}$ . Using (3.10), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle m_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}-c_{n+1}^{0}=R_{0}-\alpha q_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}\geq R_{0}-\alpha>0. $$

Thus $0\leq c_{n+1}^{0}<m_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}$ , and $T_{c_{n+1}^{0}}S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}\in\mathcal{A}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}},c_{n+1}^{0})$ . Moreover, by (3.10) and (3.14),

$$ \displaystyle m_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}} \displaystyle=R_{0}-\alpha q_{\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}}\leq R_{0}-\alpha q_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}=m_{S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}}-c_{n+1}^{0}. $$

Applying Proposition 2.3 to the pre-allocation law $S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}$ , the budget $c_{n+1}^{0}$ , and the comparison law $\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}$ , using (3.13) and (3.16), yields

$$ \mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})=T_{c_{n+1}^{0}}S_{\Delta}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}}\succsim_{2}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}. $$

By Lemma 2.6 and (3.10),

$$ R\bigl(\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})\bigr)=R(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})=R(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}})=R_{0}. $$

Therefore, $\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})\succsim_{\alpha}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}$ , which concludes the proof of (3.11). ∎

Now, let $(\mu_{t_{n}}^{\Delta})_{n=0}^{M}$ denote the discrete-time optimally controlled flow:

$$ \mu_{0}^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{0},\quad\mu_{t_{n+1}}^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu_{t_{n}}^{\Delta}). $$

#### Lemma 3.3.

It holds that

$$ \mu_{t_{n}}^{\Delta}\succsim_{\alpha}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}},\quad n=0,\ldots,M. $$

#### Proof.

This is equality when $n=0$ . Suppose it holds for some $n<M$ . Lemma 2.6 and (3.11) then give

$$ \mu_{t_{n+1}}^{\Delta}=\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu_{t_{n}}^{\Delta})\succsim_{\alpha}\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n}})\succsim_{\alpha}\widetilde{\mu}_{t_{n+1}}. $$

The claim follows by induction. ∎

In particular, $\mu_{T}^{\Delta}\succsim_{2}\widetilde{\mu}_{T}$ . Since the continuous-time admissible system was arbitrary, we have thus established

#### Corollary 3.4.

Let $f$ be any payoff in Definition 2.1, item 2. It holds that

$$ V_{f}^{\Delta}(0,\mu)\geq V_{f}(0,\mu). $$

In particular, taking $f=\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}$ gives

$$ V^{\Delta}(0,\mu)\geq V(0,\mu). $$

#### 3.2.1 Pathwise realization of the discrete cutoff flow

For clarity, we re-index and interpolate the optimally controlled probability flow in the $\Delta$ -discretized problem to a continuous-time flow:

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{(n+1)\Delta}^{\Delta} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{G}_{\Delta}(\mu_{n\Delta}^{\Delta}),\quad n\geq 0, \displaystyle\mu_{t}^{\Delta} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=S_{t-n\Delta}\mu_{n\Delta}^{\Delta},\quad t\in[n\Delta,(n+1)\Delta). $$

Then $V_{f}^{\Delta}(0,\mu_{0})=\langle\mu_{T}^{\Delta},f\rangle$ . For $n\geq 1$ , let $\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}$ be the tax threshold corresponding to the cutoff operation $T_{c_{n}^{\Delta}}S_{\Delta}\mu_{(n-1)\Delta}^{\Delta}$ , and set

$$ \kappa_{0}^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max\operatorname{supp}\mu_{0}. $$

Define the auxiliary boundary by

$$ \Lambda_{t}^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\kappa_{n}^{\Delta},\quad t\in[n\Delta,(n+1)\Delta), $$

with constant extension after $T$ whenever this is needed below.

We now give the stopped pathwise realization of this flow. Let $X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}$ and let $B$ be a Brownian motion independent of $X_{0}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle K_{t}^{\Delta} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max_{j\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\,j\Delta\leq t}\bigl(X_{0}+B_{j\Delta}-\kappa_{j}^{\Delta}\bigr)^{+}, \displaystyle\widehat{X}_{t}^{\Delta} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t}-K_{t}^{\Delta},\quad\tau^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\widehat{X}_{t}^{\Delta}\leq 0\}, $$

where we follow the convention that $\inf\varnothing\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\infty$ , and set

$$ L_{t}^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=K_{t\wedge\tau^{\Delta}}^{\Delta},\quad X_{t}^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\begin{cases}\widehat{X}_{t}^{\Delta},&t<\tau^{\Delta},\\
0,&t\geq\tau^{\Delta}.\end{cases} $$

It can be seen, jointly with the resource identity and the strict positivity of the cutoffs, that

$$ \mathcal{L}(X_{n\Delta}^{\Delta})=\mu_{n\Delta}^{\Delta},\quad\mathcal{L}(X_{t}^{\Delta})=\mu_{t}^{\Delta},\quad t\in[n\Delta,(n+1)\Delta). $$

### 3.3 Tightness of discrete-time systems

The goal of this subsection is to establish

#### Proposition 3.5.

Under Assumption 1.1, the family of auxiliary boundaries $\{\Lambda^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\Delta>0,\,T/\Delta\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is pre-compact in $\mathcal{D}((0,T+1])$ endowed with the local $M_{1}$ topology.

#### Remark 3.6.

- 1. The extension of $\Lambda^{\Delta}$ beyond time $T$ and studying them in the space $\mathcal{D}((0,T+1])$ instead of $\mathcal{D}((0,T])$ get rid of the need to analyze the limit of $\Lambda_{t}^{\Delta}$ as $t\uparrow T$ .

We start with proving some auxiliary technical results for the discrete-time systems.

#### Lemma 3.7.

Under Assumption 1.1, set $r_{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{0}-\alpha>0$ . It holds for all $\Delta>0$ and $t\geq 0$ that $\Lambda_{t}^{\Delta}\geq r_{*}$ .

#### Proof.

Because every cutoff is strictly positive, default occurs by continuous crossing, and the stopped system satisfies

$$ X_{t}^{\Delta}=X_{0}+B_{t\wedge\tau^{\Delta}}-L_{t}^{\Delta},\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

Equations (3.18)-(3.20) imply that $X_{n\Delta}^{\Delta}\leq\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}$ for $n=0,1,...,M$ . Taking expectation on both sides of the above equation for $t=n\Delta$ , and using optional stopping, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}\geq\mathbb{E}[X_{n\Delta}^{\Delta}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\mathbb{E}[L_{n\Delta}^{\Delta}]=m_{0}-\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau^{\Delta}\leq n\Delta]\geq m_{0}-\alpha=r_{*}. $$

The desired inequality then readily follows from the definition of $\Lambda^{\Delta}$ . ∎

We next prove that defaults occur at a uniformly positive rate on every positive-time interval, in the sense of the following lemma.

#### Lemma 3.8.

Under Assumption 1.1, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,T)$ there exists a constants $\beta_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that

$$ q_{n+1}^{\Delta}-q_{n}^{\Delta}\geq\beta_{\varepsilon}\Delta, $$

for every admissible mesh $\Delta$ and every $n$ satisfying

$$ \varepsilon\leq n\Delta<(n+1)\Delta\leq T. $$

#### Proof.

Choose $0<a<R<\infty$ such that $p_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{0}([a,R])>0$ , and then fix $0<r<A<\min\{a,r_{*}\}$ . Define

$$ \sigma^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}X_{t}^{\Delta}\leq r\},\quad G^{\Delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Big\{a\leq X_{0}\leq R,\ \sigma^{\Delta}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Big\}. $$

Writing $Z_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t}$ , the reflection principle gives, on $\{a\leq X_{0}\leq R\}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq t\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}Z_{t}\leq r\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{0}\right]=2\overline{\Phi}_{G}\left(\frac{X_{0}-r}{\sqrt{\varepsilon/2}}\right)\geq\rho_{\varepsilon}, $$

where

$$ \rho_{\varepsilon}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=2\overline{\Phi}_{G}\left(\frac{R-r}{\sqrt{\varepsilon/2}}\right)>0. $$

Before default, $X_{t}^{\Delta}=Z_{t}-L_{t}^{\Delta}\leq Z_{t}$ . Moreover, no allocation jump can cross the level $r$ , since every nonzero allocation jump lands at a cutoff at least $r_{*}>r$ . Thus, the controlled path reaches $r$ whenever the free path does, possibly earlier, and its first crossing of $r$ is continuous. Consequently,

$$ \mathbb{P}[G^{\Delta}]\geq p_{0}\rho_{\varepsilon}\quad\text{and}\quad X_{\sigma^{\Delta}}^{\Delta}=r\quad\text{on }G^{\Delta}. $$

Let $p_{A}$ be the Dirichlet heat kernel on $(0,A)$ and set

$$ g_{r,A}(u)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{y}p_{A}(u,r,0+),\quad u>0. $$

That is, $g_{r,A}$ is the density of exit through zero for Brownian motion started from $r$ and killed upon leaving $(0,A)$ . Positivity of $p_{A}$ , parabolic boundary regularity, and the Hopf lemma imply that $g_{r,A}$ is continuous and strictly positive on $(0,\infty)$ . Hence

$$ \underline{g}_{\varepsilon}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\min_{u\in[\varepsilon/2,T]}g_{r,A}(u)>0. $$

Fix $n$ with $\varepsilon\leq n\Delta<(n+1)\Delta\leq T$ . On the event $G^{\Delta}$ ,

$$ [n\Delta-\sigma^{\Delta},(n+1)\Delta-\sigma^{\Delta}]\subset[\varepsilon/2,T]. $$

After time $\sigma^{\Delta}$ , restrict to Brownian paths that remain in $(0,A)$ until they exit through zero. Along such paths no allocation acts, since $A<r_{*}$ lies below every cutoff. The strong Markov property at $\sigma^{\Delta}$ (formally, at $\sigma^{\Delta}\wedge\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ ) therefore shows that this killed-Brownian flux is a subflux of the actual defaults. Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle q_{n+1}^{\Delta}-q_{n}^{\Delta}=\mathbb{P}[n\Delta<\tau^{\Delta}\leq(n+1)\Delta]\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{1}_{G^{\Delta}}\int_{n\Delta-\sigma^{\Delta}}^{(n+1)\Delta-\sigma^{\Delta}}g_{r,A}(u)\,du\right]\geq p_{0}\rho_{\varepsilon}\underline{g}_{\varepsilon}\,\Delta. $$

The conclusion follows with $\beta_{\varepsilon}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=p_{0}\rho_{\varepsilon}\underline{g}_{\varepsilon}$ . ∎

We next derive a one-sided modulus for the cutoff threshold in the discrete-time systems.

#### Lemma 3.9.

For $\gamma>0$ , define

$$ \Omega_{\gamma}(h)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf_{\theta>0}\left\{\frac{\log(1+\theta/\gamma)}{2\theta}+\theta h\right\},\quad h\geq 0. $$

Let $\Delta$ be an admissible mesh and let $0\leq n<m\leq M$ . If $c_{j+1}^{\Delta}\geq\gamma\Delta$ , $j=n,\ldots,m-1$ , then $\kappa_{m}^{\Delta}-\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}\leq\Omega_{\gamma}((m-n)\Delta)$ . Moreover, $\Omega_{\gamma}$ is non-decreasing and $\Omega_{\gamma}(h)\to 0$ as $h\downarrow 0$ . Consequently, under Assumption 1.1, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,T)$ ,

$$ \kappa_{m}^{\Delta}-\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}\leq\Omega_{\gamma_{\varepsilon}}((m-n)\Delta),\quad\varepsilon\leq n\Delta<m\Delta\leq T, $$

where $\gamma_{\varepsilon}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\alpha\beta_{\varepsilon}$ and $\beta_{\varepsilon}$ is given by Lemma 3.8.

#### Proof.

For $j\geq 0$ , write

$$ C_{j}^{\Delta}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(y-x)^{+}\,\mu_{j\Delta}^{\Delta}(dy),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}, $$

and let $P_{t}$ denote the unrestricted Gaussian heat semigroup.

We first observe that

$$ C_{S_{\Delta}\mu_{j\Delta}^{\Delta}}(x)\leq P_{\Delta}C_{j}^{\Delta}(x),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}. $$

Indeed, couple the absorbed and unrestricted Brownian motions. If $\tau_{0}$ is the hitting time of zero, then bounded optional sampling gives

$$ X+B_{\Delta\wedge\tau_{0}}=\mathbb{E}\left[X+B_{\Delta}\mid\mathcal{F}_{\Delta\wedge\tau_{0}}\right]. $$

Jensen’s inequality for $z\mapsto(z-x)^{+}$ , followed by Brownian symmetry, proves the claim.

The cutoff identity also holds on the whole real line:

$$ C_{j+1}^{\Delta}(x)=\left(C_{S_{\Delta}\mu_{j\Delta}^{\Delta}}(x)-c_{j+1}^{\Delta}\right)^{+},\quad x\in\mathbb{R}. $$

For $x<\kappa_{j+1}^{\Delta}$ , this follows from

$$ (\min\{y,\kappa_{j+1}^{\Delta}\}-x)^{+}=(y-x)^{+}-(y-\kappa_{j+1}^{\Delta})^{+}, $$

while for $x\geq\kappa_{j+1}^{\Delta}$ both sides vanish. Consequently, if $c_{j+1}^{\Delta}\geq\gamma\Delta$ , then

$$ C_{j+1}^{\Delta}\leq\mathcal{Q}_{\gamma,\Delta}C_{j}^{\Delta},\quad\mathcal{Q}_{\gamma,\Delta}f\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(P_{\Delta}f-\gamma\Delta)^{+}, $$

pointwise on $\mathbb{R}$ . Notice also that $\mathcal{Q}_{\gamma,\Delta}$ is order preserving. Since $\mu_{n\Delta}^{\Delta}$ is supported in $[0,\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}]$ ,

$$ C_{n}^{\Delta}(x)\leq(\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}-x)^{+},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}. $$

Fix $\theta>0$ and define

$$ F_{\theta}(y)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\gamma}{2\theta^{2}}\big(e^{2\theta y}-1-2\theta y\big),\quad b_{\theta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{2\theta}\log\left(1+\frac{\theta}{\gamma}\right). $$

Then $F_{\theta}$ is nonnegative and convex,

$$ F_{\theta}(0)=F_{\theta}^{\prime}(0)=0,\quad F_{\theta}^{\prime}(b_{\theta})=1, $$

and hence

$$ F_{\theta}(y)\geq(y-b_{\theta})^{+},\quad y\geq 0. $$

Therefore,

$$ W_{\theta}(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=F_{\theta}\left((\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}+b_{\theta}+\theta t-x)^{+}\right) $$

satisfies

$$ C_{n}^{\Delta}(x)\leq W_{\theta}(0,x),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}. $$

A direct calculation gives

$$ \left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)W_{\theta}=-\gamma\,\mathbf{1}_{\{x<\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}+b_{\theta}+\theta t\}}\geq-\gamma $$

in the distributional sense. There is no interface measure because $F_{\theta}(0)=F_{\theta}^{\prime}(0)=0$ . The heat-semigroup comparison therefore yields

$$ \mathcal{Q}_{\gamma,\Delta}W_{\theta}(t,\cdot)\leq W_{\theta}(t+\Delta,\cdot). $$

By monotonicity of $\mathcal{Q}_{\gamma,\Delta}$ , induction gives

$$ C_{n+\ell}^{\Delta}(x)\leq W_{\theta}(\ell\Delta,x),\quad 0\leq\ell\leq m-n. $$

The right-hand side vanishes whenever $x\geq\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}+b_{\theta}+\theta\ell\Delta$ . Hence,

$$ \mathrm{supp}\,\mu_{(n+\ell)\Delta}^{\Delta}\subset\left[0,\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}+b_{\theta}+\theta\ell\Delta\right]. $$

Since $c_{m}^{\Delta}\geq\gamma\Delta>0$ , the cutoff operation at time $m\Delta$ places positive mass at $\kappa_{m}^{\Delta}$ . Thus

$$ \kappa_{m}^{\Delta}=\max\mathrm{supp}\,\mu_{m\Delta}^{\Delta}. $$

Taking $\ell=m-n$ gives

$$ \kappa_{m}^{\Delta}-\kappa_{n}^{\Delta}\leq\frac{\log(1+\theta/\gamma)}{2\theta}+\theta(m-n)\Delta. $$

Minimizing over $\theta>0$ proves the desired bound. Finally, $\Omega_{\gamma}$ is non-decreasing because each function inside the infimum is non-decreasing in $h$ . For every fixed $\theta>0$ ,

$$ 0\leq\limsup_{h\downarrow 0}\Omega_{\gamma}(h)\leq\frac{\log(1+\theta/\gamma)}{2\theta}. $$

Letting $\theta\to\infty$ proves $\Omega_{\gamma}(h)\to 0$ . For the final assertion, Lemma 3.8 and the exact balance give

$$ c_{j+1}^{\Delta}=\alpha(q_{j+1}^{\Delta}-q_{j}^{\Delta})\geq\alpha\beta_{\varepsilon}\Delta=\gamma_{\varepsilon}\Delta,\quad j=n,\ldots,m-1. $$

The preceding deterministic comparison applies. ∎

### 3.4 Limiting boundary and control in continuous time

#### Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Fix $f$ as in item 2 of Definition 2.1, and choose admissible meshes $\Delta_{k}\downarrow 0$ such that

$$ V_{f}^{\Delta_{k}}(0,\mu_{0})\to\limsup_{\Delta\downarrow 0}V_{f}^{\Delta}(0,\mu_{0}). $$

Put $M_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=T/\Delta_{k}$ , write $\Lambda^{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Lambda^{\Delta_{k}}|_{[0,T]}$ , set $\Lambda_{T}^{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\kappa_{M_{k}}^{\Delta_{k}}$ , and denote its constant extension to $[0,T+1]$ by $\overline{\Lambda}^{k}$ .

#### Extraction of the boundary.

Proposition 3.5 gives, along a subsequence, a deterministic $\overline{\Lambda}\in\mathcal{D}((0,T+1])$ such that

$$ \overline{\Lambda}^{k}\to\overline{\Lambda}\quad\text{locally in $M_{1}$ on $(0,T+1]$}. $$

The limit is constant on $[T,T+1]$ . Thus, with $\Lambda\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\overline{\Lambda}|_{(0,T]}$ , the standard extension–restriction property of $M_{1}$ gives

$$ \Lambda^{k}\to\Lambda\quad\text{in $M_{1}([\varepsilon,T])$} $$

whenever $\varepsilon>0$ is a continuity point of $\Lambda$ . Moreover, Lemma 3.7 and passage to the limit give, with $r_{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{0}-\alpha>0$ ,

$$ \Lambda_{t}^{k}\geq r_{*}\quad(0\leq t\leq T),\quad\Lambda_{t}\geq r_{*}\quad(0<t\leq T). $$

Use a common $X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}$ and Brownian motion $B$ , independent of $X_{0}$ , and set

$$ Y_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t},\quad\pi_{k}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Delta_{k}\Big\lfloor\frac{t}{\Delta_{k}}\Big\rfloor,\quad Y_{t}^{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Y_{\pi_{k}(t)}. $$

The realization in (3.18)– (3.20) reads

$$ \displaystyle K_{t}^{k} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}(Y_{s}^{k}-\Lambda_{s}^{k})^{+}, \displaystyle Z_{t}^{k} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Y_{t}-K_{t}^{k}, \displaystyle\tau^{k} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}Z_{t}^{k}\leq 0\}, \displaystyle L_{t}^{k} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=K_{t\wedge\tau^{k}}^{k},\quad X_{t}^{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Z_{t}^{k}\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\tau^{k}\}}, $$

where $\inf\varnothing=\infty$ . In particular, $\mathcal{L}(X_{t}^{k})=\mu_{t}^{\Delta_{k}}$ . Exact balance at grid times and constancy between grid times yield

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}^{k}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau^{k}\leq\pi_{k}(t)],\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

#### The initial layer and the reflection limit.

For $0<r<r_{*}$ , every positive tax leaves the reserve at a cutoff at least $r_{*}$ , whereas between tax times the regulator is constant. Consequently,

$$ \{\tau^{k}\leq h\}\subset\{X_{0}\leq r\}\cup\{\operatorname{osc}_{[0,h]}B\geq r\}. $$

The reflection principle therefore gives

$$ \sup_{k}\mathbb{P}[\tau^{k}\leq h]\leq\rho_{\mu_{0}}(h)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf_{0<r<r_{*}}\Big\{\mu_{0}([0,r])+4\exp\Big(-\frac{r^{2}}{8h}\Big)\Big\}, $$

and $\rho_{\mu_{0}}(h)\to 0$ as $h\downarrow 0$ , since $\mu_{0}(\{0\})=0$ . Let $H_{T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+\sup_{s\leq T}|B_{s}|\in L^{1}$ . Then $K_{t}^{k}\leq H_{T}$ , and

$$ K_{h}^{k}\leq L_{h}^{k}+H_{T}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau^{k}\leq h\}}. $$

Together with (3.29), this gives

$$ \sup_{k}\mathbb{E}[K_{h}^{k}]\leq\alpha\rho_{\mu_{0}}(h)+\sup_{\mathbb{P}(A)\leq\rho_{\mu_{0}}(h)}\mathbb{E}[H_{T}\mathbf{1}_{A}]=\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\eta_{\mu_{0}}(h), $$

where $\eta_{\mu_{0}}(h)\to 0$ as $h\downarrow 0$ . Define

$$ K_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=0,\quad K_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0<s\leq t}(Y_{s}-\Lambda_{s})^{+},\quad 0<t\leq T. $$

For a continuity point $h>0$ of $\Lambda$ , set

$$ K_{t}^{k,h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{h\leq s\leq t}(Y_{s}^{k}-\Lambda_{s}^{k})^{+},\quad K_{t}^{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{h\leq s\leq t}(Y_{s}-\Lambda_{s})^{+}. $$

Addition of a continuous path and the positive running-supremum map are continuous in scalar $M_{1}$ ; for the latter, take running suprema of the spatial components of ordered parametric representations. Since $Y^{k}\to Y$ uniformly almost surely,

$$ K^{k,h}\to K^{h}\quad\text{almost surely in $M_{1}([h,T])$}. $$

If $0<r<h$ are continuity points of $\Lambda$ , then $K_{h}^{k,r}\to K_{h}^{r}$ almost surely. Fatou’s lemma, (3.31), and then monotone convergence as $r\downarrow 0$ show that $\mathbb{E}[K_{h}]\leq\eta_{\mu_{0}}(h)$ . Letting $h\downarrow 0$ through continuity points gives

$$ K_{0+}=0\quad\text{almost surely}. $$

Thus $K\in\mathcal{D}([0,T])$ . Now, for continuity points $0<h<\delta$ of $\Lambda$ ,

$$ \displaystyle d_{M_{1},[\delta,T]}(K^{k},K) \displaystyle\leq K_{h}^{k}+d_{M_{1},[\delta,T]}(K^{k,h},K^{h})+K_{h}. $$

Equations (3.31) and (3.33), followed by $h\downarrow 0$ , imply

$$ K^{k}\to K\quad\text{in probability in $M_{1}([\delta,T])$} $$

for every positive continuity point $\delta$ of $\Lambda$ .

#### Absorption and exact balance.

Set

$$ Z_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Y_{t}-K_{t},\quad\tau\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}Z_{t}\leq 0\},\quad L_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=K_{t\wedge\tau},\quad X_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Z_{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{t<\tau\}}, $$

again with $\inf\varnothing=\infty$ . From (3.35),

$$ Z^{k}\to Z\quad\text{locally in $M_{1}$ on $(0,T]$, in probability}. $$

Moreover, (3.34) gives $Z_{0+}=X_{0}>0$ almost surely. Hence $\tau>0$ almost surely and $\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq h]\to 0$ as $h\downarrow 0$ . Since $\Lambda$ is deterministic, $K,Z$ are adapted and $\tau$ is a stopping time. At every jump time of $K$ ,

$$ \Delta K_{t}=(Z_{t-}-\Lambda_{t})^{+},\quad Z_{t}=Z_{t-}\wedge\Lambda_{t}. $$

The measure $dK$ is supported, with the appropriate one-sided value at jumps, on the contact set $Z=\Lambda$ . Hence $K$ is constant on any interval on which $Z_{s}\vee Z_{s-}<r_{*}$ for every $s$ . Since $Z$ has no upward jumps and (3.38) excludes a regulator jump to or through zero,

$$ Z_{\tau-}=Z_{\tau}=0,\quad\Delta K_{\tau}=0\quad\text{on }\{\tau\leq T\}. $$

On $\{\tau<T\}$ , strong Markov and the local constancy of $K$ give

$$ \inf_{\tau<s<(\tau+\varepsilon)\wedge T}Z_{s}<0\quad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0 $$

almost surely. The same local constancy shows that

$$ \mathbb{P}[\tau=t]=0,\qquad 0<t\leq T. $$

Indeed, on $\{\tau=t\}$ , $K$ is constant on $[t-1/n,t]$ for some $n>1/t$ , so

$$ \{\tau=t\}\subset\bigcup_{n>1/t}\{Z_{t-1/n}+B_{t}-B_{t-1/n}=0\}. $$

Each event on the right is null after conditioning on $\mathcal{F}_{t-1/n}$ .

We claim that, whenever $t_{k}\to t\in(0,T]$ ,

$$ \tau^{k}\wedge t_{k}\to\tau\wedge t\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau^{k}\leq t_{k}\}}\to\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq t\}},\quad\text{in probability}. $$

From every subsequence, a diagonal extraction in (3.37) gives almost-sure $M_{1}$ -convergence on every $[a,T]$ , $a\in\mathcal{D}$ . The completed graph of $Z$ is uniformly separated from zero on compact intervals strictly before $\tau$ , because $Z$ is positive there and has no upward jumps. This gives the lower bound for the hitting times; (3.39) gives the upper bound through a negative continuity point immediately after any hit before $T$ . If $\tau=\infty$ , the completed graph on $[a,T]$ is uniformly positive. All bracketing points here are chosen from $\mathcal{D}$ . Finally let $a\downarrow 0$ , using (3.30) and $\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq a]\to 0$ . This proves convergence of the capped hitting times and hence the first line of (3.41). For the indicators, on $\{\tau<t\}$ choose a negative continuity point $s\in\mathcal{D}\cap(\tau,t)$ ; then $\tau^{k}<t_{k}$ eventually. If non-decreasing $k_{n}\to k$ in $M_{1}$ , $s_{n}\to s$ , and $k$ is continuous at $s$ , then $k_{n}(s_{n})\to k(s)$ . Applying this standard fact to (3.35) and (3.41), noting that $K$ is continuous at every continuity point of $\Lambda$ and at $\tau$ , gives

$$ L_{t}^{k}\to L_{t}\quad\text{in probability} $$

at every continuity point $t\in(0,T)$ of $\Lambda$ . At time $T$ , use $\tau^{k}\to\tau$ and moving-time evaluation on $\{\tau<T\}$ , and endpoint $M_{1}$ -convergence on $\{\tau>T\}$ . Together with the indicator convergence, this gives

$$ L_{T}^{k}\to L_{T},\quad X_{T}^{k}\to X_{T},\quad\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau^{k}\leq T\}}\to\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq T\}}\quad\text{in probability}, $$

where $\{\tau=T\}$ is null by (3.40). Because $L_{t}^{k}\leq H_{T}$ , the family is uniformly integrable. Therefore, at every continuity point $t\in(0,T)$ of $\Lambda$ ,

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t],\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

$$ \Delta L_{t}=X_{t-}-\Lambda_{t}\leq X_{t-}-r_{*}<X_{t-}, $$

while $\Delta L_{\tau}=0$ . Thus, $(X,B,L,\tau)\in\mathfrak{A}(\mu_{0})$ .

#### Terminal payoff and conclusion.

To account for the possible jump of $f$ at zero, write

$$ J_{f}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=f(0+)-f(0),\quad\overline{f}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=f(x)-f(0)-J_{f}\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}(x). $$

Then $f=f(0)+J_{f}\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}+\overline{f}$ , where $\overline{f}$ is continuous and has at most linear growth. Since

$$ 0\leq X_{T}^{k}\leq(X_{0}+B_{T})^{+}, $$

and

$$ |\overline{f}(X_{T}^{k})|\leq C\bigl(1+(X_{0}+B_{T})^{+}\bigr), $$

$$ \mathbb{E}[f(X_{T}^{k})]\to\mathbb{E}[f(X_{T})]. $$

$$ V_{f}(0,\mu_{0})\geq\mathbb{E}[f(X_{T})]=\lim_{k\to\infty}V_{f}^{\Delta_{k}}(0,\mu_{0})=\limsup_{\Delta\downarrow 0}V_{f}^{\Delta}(0,\mu_{0}). $$
