$$ \lim_{\Delta\downarrow 0}V_{f}^{\Delta}(0,\mu_{0})=V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}), $$

and completes the proof. ∎

## 4 The Associated Free Boundary Problem

This section studies the probabilistic free boundary formulation satisfied by the limiting optimal flow constructed in Section 3. We introduce the probabilistic notion, establish its structural properties, and derive an augmented call-function formulation that yields stability and uniqueness. We then prove positive-time classical regularity, recovering the free boundary system (1.1) from the probabilistic construction. The section concludes with uniqueness of the continuous-time optimal flow.

### 4.1 Definition of probabilistic solutions

#### Definition 4.1 (Probabilistic solution with a local boundary).

Fix $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ with $\mu_{0}(\{0\})=0$ . Let $\Lambda\in D((0,T];(0,\infty))$ be deterministic, let $X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}$ , and let $B$ be a Brownian motion independent of $X_{0}$ . Set $K_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=0$ , $\widetilde{X}_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}$ , and, for $t>0$ , define

$$ K_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0<s\leq t}(X_{0}+B_{s}-\Lambda_{s})^{+},\quad\widetilde{X}_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t}-K_{t}. $$

Let $\tau\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\widetilde{X}_{t}\leq 0\}$ with the convention that $\inf\varnothing\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\infty$ , and set

$$ L_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=K_{t\wedge\tau},\quad X_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t\wedge\tau}-L_{t},\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

We call $(X,\Lambda)$ a probabilistic solution to the free boundary problem (1.1) if

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]\,\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

#### Lemma 4.2 (Classical solutions induce probabilistic solutions).

Suppose $(u,\Lambda)$ is a classical solution to the free boundary problem (1.1) on $[0,T]$ , with $\Lambda\in C^{1}([0,T];(0,\infty))$ , and suppose that

$$ \displaystyle u(0,\cdot)\geq 0,\quad\operatorname{supp}u(0,\cdot)\subset[0,\Lambda_{0}],\quad\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{0}}u(0,x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1. $$

Let $X_{0}$ be a random variable with density $u(0,\cdot)$ , and let $B$ be a Brownian motion independent of $X_{0}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle K_{t} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{s\in[0,t]}(X_{0}+B_{s}-\Lambda_{s})^{+},\quad\widetilde{X}_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X_{0}+B_{t}-K_{t}, \displaystyle\tau \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t\in[0,T]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\,\widetilde{X}_{t}\leq 0\},\quad\inf\varnothing\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\infty, \displaystyle L_{t} \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=K_{t\wedge\tau},\quad X_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{X}_{t},&t<\tau,\\
0,&t\geq\tau.\end{cases} $$

Then $(X,\Lambda)$ is a probabilistic solution in the sense of Definition 4.1. Moreover, for every $t\in[0,T]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}[X_{t}\in\mathrm{d}x]=\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]\,\delta_{0}(\mathrm{d}x)+u(t,x)\mathbf{1}_{(0,\Lambda_{t})}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. $$

#### Proof.

Since $X_{0}\leq\Lambda_{0}$ almost surely, including $s=0$ in the definition of $K$ does not change the regulator from Definition 4.1. Continuity of $B$ and $\Lambda$ gives $K_{0+}=L_{0+}=0$ . The running-supremum formula also shows that $K$ is continuous and non-decreasing, that $\widetilde{X}_{t}\leq\Lambda_{t}$ , and that $dK_{t}$ is carried by $\{\widetilde{X}_{t}=\Lambda_{t}\}$ . Because $X_{0}>0$ almost surely, $\widetilde{X}_{\tau}=0$ on the event $\{\tau\leq T\}$ . Consequently,

$$ X_{t}=\widetilde{X}_{t\wedge\tau}=X_{0}+B_{t\wedge\tau}-K_{t\wedge\tau}=X_{0}+B_{t\wedge\tau}-L_{t}. $$

Fix $t\in(0,T]$ . Let $g$ be smooth, vanish near zero, and be constant near $\Lambda_{t}$ . Let $\psi$ solve the backward mixed-boundary problem

$$ \begin{cases}\partial_{s}\psi+\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\psi=0,&0\leq s<t,\quad 0<x<\Lambda_{s},\\
\psi(s,0)=0,\qquad\partial_{x}\psi(s,\Lambda_{s})=0,&0\leq s\leq t,\\
\psi(t,x)=g(x),&0\leq x\leq\Lambda_{t}.\end{cases} $$

Applying Itô’s formula to $s\mapsto\psi(s,\widetilde{X}_{s})$ up to $t\wedge\tau$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\psi(t\wedge\tau,\widetilde{X}_{t\wedge\tau}) \displaystyle=\psi(0,X_{0})+\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau}\left(\partial_{s}\psi+\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\psi\right)(s,\widetilde{X}_{s})\,ds \displaystyle+\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau}\partial_{x}\psi(s,\widetilde{X}_{s})\,dB_{s}-\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau}\partial_{x}\psi(s,\widetilde{X}_{s})\,dK_{s}. $$

The first integral vanishes by the backward equation. Since $dK_{s}$ is carried by $\{\widetilde{X}_{s}=\Lambda_{s}\}$ ,

$$ \int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau}\partial_{x}\psi(s,\widetilde{X}_{s})\,dK_{s}=\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau}\partial_{x}\psi(s,\Lambda_{s})\,dK_{s}=0. $$

Moreover, $\psi(t\wedge\tau,\widetilde{X}_{t\wedge\tau})=g(X_{t})$ , because it equals $g(\widetilde{X}_{t})=g(X_{t})$ on $\{\tau>t\}$ , whereas on $\{\tau\leq t\}$ both sides equal zero by $\widetilde{X}_{\tau}=X_{t}=0$ and $\psi(\tau,0)=g(0)=0$ . Taking expectations therefore yields

$$ \mathbb{E}[g(X_{t})]=\mathbb{E}[\psi(0,X_{0})]=\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{0}}\psi(0,x)u(0,x)\,dx. $$

On the other hand, Green’s identity and the boundary conditions in (1.1) give

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{s}}\psi(s,x)u(s,x)\,dx=\dot{\Lambda}_{s}\psi(s,\Lambda_{s})u(s,\Lambda_{s})+\frac{1}{2}\bigl[\psi\,\partial_{x}u-(\partial_{x}\psi)u\bigr]_{x=0}^{x=\Lambda_{s}}=0. $$

Therefore,

$$ \mathbb{E}[g(X_{t})]=\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{t}}g(x)u(t,x)\,dx. $$

Such functions $g$ are uniformly dense among continuous functions on $[0,\Lambda_{t}]$ that vanish at zero. Hence

$$ \mathbb{P}[X_{t}\in dx]=q_{t}\delta_{0}(dx)+u(t,x)\mathbf{1}_{(0,\Lambda_{t})}(x)\,dx, $$

where

$$ q_{t}=\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]=1-\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{t}}u(t,x)\,dx. $$

It remains to verify the exact balance equation. Put

$$ M_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{t}}u(t,x)\,dx,\quad m_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{t}}x\,u(t,x)\,dx. $$

Leibniz’ rule, the heat equation, and the first upper-boundary condition give

$$ \dot{M}_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x}u(t,0),\quad\dot{m}_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}u(t,\Lambda_{t}). $$

Since $M_{0}=1$ ,

$$ q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\partial_{x}u(s,0)\,ds. $$

Furthermore, optional stopping and the law identity give

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\mathbb{E}[X_{t}]=m_{0}-m_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}u(s,\Lambda_{s})\,ds. $$

Using $u(s,\Lambda_{s})=\alpha\partial_{x}u(s,0)$ , we conclude that

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\frac{\alpha}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\partial_{x}u(s,0)\,ds=\alpha q_{t}=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]. $$

Therefore, $(X,\Lambda)$ is a probabilistic solution, and the asserted law formula follows. ∎

### 4.2 Analytical properties of probabilistic solutions

Throughout this subsection, let $(X,\Lambda)$ be a probabilistic solution on $[0,T]$ in the sense of Definition 4.1, let

$$ \mu_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t}),\quad\tau\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\{t>0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}X_{t}\leq 0\}, $$

and suppose that $\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]>\alpha$ . Under Assumption 1.1, $r_{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\alpha>0$ . In a similar fashion to Lemma 3.7, we can prove

#### Lemma 4.3 (Uniform positivity of the free boundary).

Under Assumption 1.1, $\Lambda_{t}\geq r_{*}$ for all $t\in(0,T]$ .

#### Proof.

Optional stopping gives $\mathbb{E}[B_{t\wedge\tau}]=0$ . Using the exact balance equation $\mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]$ , we obtain

$$ \mathbb{E}[X_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t]\geq r_{*}. $$

On the other hand, the Skorokhod representation implies that $0\leq X_{t}\leq\Lambda_{t}$ a.s. Consequently,

$$ \Lambda_{t}\geq\mathbb{E}[X_{t}]\geq r_{*}. $$

∎

#### Lemma 4.4 (Interior reachability).

Let $0<r<t\leq T$ , and let $J$ be a nonempty open interval such that $J\subset\big(0,\inf_{s\in[r,t]}\Lambda_{s}\big)$ . For every $x\in(0,\Lambda_{r}]$ , the reflected process restarted from $x$ at time $r$ satisfies

$$ \mathbb{P}_{r,x}[X_{t}\in J,\ \tau>t]>0. $$

Moreover, if $J\subset\big(0,\inf_{s\in[r,t)}\Lambda_{s}\big)$ , then

$$ \mathbb{P}_{r,x}[X_{t-}\in J,\ \tau\geq t]>0. $$

#### Proof.

Set

$$ h\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=t-r,\quad W_{u}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=B_{r+u}-B_{r},\quad\lambda(u)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Lambda_{r+u},\quad b\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf_{0\leq u\leq h}\lambda(u)>0. $$

For $\varphi\in D([0,h])$ , write

$$ \Gamma_{\lambda}(\varphi)(u)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\varphi(u)-\sup_{0\leq v\leq u}\bigl(\varphi(v)-\lambda(v)\bigr)^{+}. $$

Thus, the restarted, unabsorbed reflected trajectory is $Y\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Gamma_{\lambda}(x+W)$ . For fixed $\lambda$ , the Skorokhod map satisfies

$$ \|\Gamma_{\lambda}(\varphi)-\Gamma_{\lambda}(\widetilde{\varphi})\|_{\infty}\leq 2\|\varphi-\widetilde{\varphi}\|_{\infty}. $$

Fix $z\in J$ . For $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$ , define

$$ \varphi^{\theta}(u)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=x+\theta u,\quad y^{\theta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Gamma_{\lambda}(\varphi^{\theta}),\quad F(\theta)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=y^{\theta}(h). $$

Estimate (4.3) shows that $F$ is continuous. Choose $\theta_{-}<0$ so that $x+\theta_{-}h<z$ . Since the regulator is non-negative,

$$ F(\theta_{-})\leq x+\theta_{-}h<z. $$

On the other hand, for $\theta_{+}\geq 0$ sufficiently large, $x+\theta_{+}h>z$ . Since $\varphi^{\theta_{+}}$ is non-decreasing and $\lambda\geq b$ ,

$$ \displaystyle F(\theta_{+})\geq x+\theta_{+}h-\bigl(x+\theta_{+}h-b\bigr)^{+}=\min\{x+\theta_{+}h,b\}>z. $$

The intermediate value theorem therefore gives $\theta_{*}\in(\theta_{-},\theta_{+})$ such that

$$ y^{\theta_{*}}(h)=F(\theta_{*})=z. $$

The whole path $y^{\theta_{*}}$ stays strictly positive. Indeed, if $\theta_{*}<0$ , then $\varphi^{\theta_{*}}$ is non-increasing while its regulator is non-decreasing; hence $y^{\theta_{*}}$ is non-increasing and

$$ y^{\theta_{*}}(u)\geq y^{\theta_{*}}(h)=z>0. $$

If $\theta_{*}\geq 0$ , then, for every $u\in[0,h]$ ,

$$ y^{\theta_{*}}(u)\geq x+\theta_{*}u-\bigl(x+\theta_{*}u-b\bigr)^{+}=\min\{x+\theta_{*}u,b\}\geq\min\{x,b\}>0. $$

Consequently,

$$ m\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf_{0\leq u\leq h}y^{\theta_{*}}(u)>0. $$

Choose $\eta>0$ such that $2\eta<\min\{m,\operatorname{dist}(z,J^{c})\}$ . On the event

$$ A_{\eta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\{\sup_{0\leq u\leq h}|W_{u}-\theta_{*}u|<\eta\right\}, $$

estimate (4.3) gives $\|Y-y^{\theta_{*}}\|_{\infty}<2\eta$ . Thus, $Y$ remains strictly positive and $Y_{h}\in J$ . Therefore,

$$ A_{\eta}\subseteq\{X_{t}\in J,\ \tau>t\}. $$

Since Wiener measure has full support on $C_{0}([0,h])$ , $\mathbb{P}_{r,x}[A_{\eta}]>0$ , proving the first assertion.

For the second assertion, replace the terminal value of the shifted boundary by setting

$$ \lambda^{-}(u)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\begin{cases}\Lambda_{r+u},&0\leq u<h,\\
\Lambda_{t-},&u=h.\end{cases} $$

Then

$$ \inf_{0\leq u\leq h}\lambda^{-}(u)=\inf_{s\in[r,t)}\Lambda_{s}, $$

so the preceding argument applies to $\lambda^{-}$ . Moreover, for every continuous $\varphi$ ,

$$ \sup_{0\leq v\leq h}\bigl(\varphi(v)-\lambda^{-}(v)\bigr)^{+}=\sup_{0\leq v<h}\bigl(\varphi(v)-\Lambda_{r+v}\bigr)^{+}, $$

because the term at $v=h$ is the limit of the terms as $v\uparrow h$ . Hence,

$$ \Gamma_{\lambda^{-}}(\varphi)(h)=\lim_{u\uparrow h}\Gamma_{\lambda}(\varphi)(u). $$

For $\varphi=x+W$ , this is precisely the left limit of the restarted reflected process at time $t$ . On the positive-probability tube constructed above, the process remains positive on $[r,t)$ , so $\tau\geq t$ and the terminal value is $X_{t-}\in J$ . This proves the second assertion. ∎

#### Lemma 4.5 (Absence of upward jumps).

For every $t\in(0,T)$ , $\Lambda_{t}\leq\Lambda_{t-}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $t_{0}\in(0,T)$ and suppose, towards a contradiction, that $\delta\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Lambda_{t_{0}}-\Lambda_{t_{0}-}>0$ . Choose

$$ 0<\eta<\min\left\{r_{*},\frac{\delta}{2}\right\},\quad J\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left(\frac{\eta}{2},\eta\right). $$

Set $r\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=t_{0}/2$ . By (4.1), $\mathbb{P}[X_{r}>0]>0$ , while $J\subset\left(0,\inf_{s\in[r,t_{0}]}\Lambda_{s}\right)$ . Conditioning on $X_{r}$ and applying Lemma 4.4 therefore gives

$$ \mathbb{P}[X_{t_{0}}\in J,\ \tau>t_{0}]=\mu_{t_{0}}(J)>0. $$

By the right-continuity of $\Lambda$ , there exists $h_{0}\in(0,T-t_{0}]$ such that

$$ \Lambda_{t_{0}+u}\geq\Lambda_{t_{0}-}+\frac{\delta}{2},\quad 0\leq u\leq h_{0}. $$

An upward jump of the boundary does not increase the regulator, so $L_{t_{0}}=L_{t_{0}-}$ . Moreover, $X_{t_{0}}\leq\Lambda_{t_{0}-}$ on $\{\tau>t_{0}\}$ . Let $W_{u}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=B_{t_{0}+u}-B_{t_{0}}$ . For $0<h\leq h_{0}$ , the Skorokhod representation and (4.4) give

$$ L_{t_{0}+h}-L_{t_{0}}\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau>t_{0}\}}\sup_{0\leq u\leq h}\bigl(X_{t_{0}}+W_{u}-\Lambda_{t_{0}+u}\bigr)^{+}\leq\left(\sup_{0\leq u\leq h}W_{u}-\frac{\delta}{2}\right)^{+}. $$

Set $M_{h}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq u\leq h}W_{u}$ . Since $M_{h}\overset{d}{=}\sqrt{h}\,|N(0,1)|$ , the reflection principle gives

$$ \mathbb{E}\big[L_{t_{0}+h}-L_{t_{0}}\big]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[M_{h}\mathbf{1}_{\{M_{h}>\delta/2\}}\right]\leq C\sqrt{h}\exp\left(-\frac{\delta^{2}}{8h}\right) $$

for all sufficiently small $h>0$ .

Recall that $\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}$ denotes the standard Gaussian upper tail. Conditional on $X_{t_{0}}=x>0$ , the event $\left\{\inf_{0\leq u\leq h}(x+W_{u})\leq 0\right\}$ forces default by time $t_{0}+h$ , since the control can only decrease the state. Hence, the reflection principle and Mills’ inequality yield

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}[t_{0}<\tau\leq t_{0}+h]\geq\int_{J}2\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{h}}\right)\mu_{t_{0}}(dx)\geq 2\mu_{t_{0}}(J)\cdot\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\left(\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{h}}\right)\geq c\sqrt{h}\exp\left(-\frac{\eta^{2}}{2h}\right) $$

for all sufficiently small $h>0$ and some $c>0$ . Finally, exact balance gives

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[L_{t_{0}+h}-L_{t_{0}}\bigr]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[t_{0}<\tau\leq t_{0}+h]. $$

Combining (4.5)–(4.7) gives

$$ \alpha c\exp\left(\frac{\delta^{2}/8-\eta^{2}/2}{h}\right)\leq C $$

for all sufficiently small $h>0$ , which is impossible because $\eta<\delta/2$ . Therefore, $\Lambda_{t_{0}}\leq\Lambda_{t_{0}-}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.6 (Absence of downward jumps).

For every $t\in(0,T]$ , $\Lambda_{t}\geq\Lambda_{t-}$ .

#### Proof.

The running-supremum representation shows that, before absorption, the continuous part of $dL$ is carried by the contact set $\{X=\Lambda\}$ . Moreover, for every $s\in(0,T]$ ,

$$ \Delta L_{s}=\bigl(X_{s-}-\Lambda_{s}\bigr)^{+},\quad X_{s}=X_{s-}-\Delta L_{s}=X_{s-}\wedge\Lambda_{s}. $$

By Lemma 4.3, every increase of $L$ leaves the reflected state at least $r_{*}>0$ . Thus, the regulator cannot cause default, and the continuity of $B$ gives $X_{t-}=X_{t}=0$ on $\{\tau=t\}$ . Fix $t\in(0,T]$ . For every integer $n>1/t$ , set $r_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=t-1/n$ and define

$$ A_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\{\tau=t,\sup_{s\in[r_{n},t]}X_{s}<\frac{r_{*}}{2}\right\}. $$

Then $\{\tau=t\}=\bigcup_{n>1/t}A_{n}$ . On $A_{n}$ , the support property of $dL^{c}$ and the jump formula (4.8) imply that $L$ is constant on $[r_{n},t]$ , and therefore $0=X_{t}=X_{r_{n}}+B_{t}-B_{r_{n}}$ . Conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_{r_{n}}$ , the increment $B_{t}-B_{r_{n}}$ has a density, so $\mathbb{P}[A_{n}]=0$ . Taking the countable union gives

$$ \mathbb{P}[\tau=t]=0,\quad t\in(0,T]. $$

Since $L$ is non-decreasing, monotone convergence and the defining balance relation give

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t-}]=\lim_{s\uparrow t}\mathbb{E}[L_{s}]=\alpha\lim_{s\uparrow t}\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq s]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau<t]. $$

Consequently, by (4.9),

$$ \mathbb{E}[\Delta L_{t}]=\alpha\mathbb{P}[\tau=t]=0. $$

Since $\Delta L_{t}\geq 0$ , it follows that $\Delta L_{t}=0$ almost surely. Suppose now, toward a contradiction, that $\delta\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Lambda_{t-}-\Lambda_{t}>0$ . Choose

$$ J\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left(\Lambda_{t}+\frac{\delta}{3},\Lambda_{t}+\frac{2\delta}{3}\right)\subset(\Lambda_{t},\Lambda_{t-}). $$

Since $\Lambda$ has a left limit at $t$ , there exists $r<t$ , sufficiently close to $t$ , such that

$$ \inf_{q\in[r,t)}\Lambda_{q}>\sup J. $$

Moreover, (4.1) implies $\mathbb{P}[X_{r}>0]>0$ . Applying the left-limit assertion of Lemma 4.4 conditionally on $X_{r}$ yields

$$ \mathbb{P}\big[X_{t-}\in J,\ \tau\geq t\big]>0. $$

On this event, (4.8) gives $\Delta L_{t}>\delta/3$ , contradicting $\Delta L_{t}=0$ almost surely. Therefore, $\Lambda_{t}\geq\Lambda_{t-}$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.7 (Canonical terminal normalization).

Lemma 4.6 gives $\Lambda_{T}\geq\Lambda_{T-}$ . Moreover, by the continuity of $B$ and the existence of the left limit of $\Lambda$ ,

$$ (X_{0}+B_{T}-\Lambda_{T-})^{+}=\lim_{s\uparrow T}(X_{0}+B_{s}-\Lambda_{s})^{+}\leq K_{T-}. $$

Thus, neither the original terminal value $\Lambda_{T}$ nor its replacement by $\Lambda_{T-}$ contributes a new maximum to the running-supremum formula for $K_{T}$ . Consequently, replacing $\Lambda_{T}$ by $\Lambda_{T-}$ leaves $K$ , $\widetilde{X}$ , $\tau$ , $L$ , and $X$ unchanged, and hence preserves the probabilistic-solution property. We henceforth adopt the canonical normalization

$$ \Lambda_{T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Lambda_{T-}. $$

Together with Lemmas 4.5 and 4.6, this implies that $\Lambda$ is actually continuous on $(0,T]$ .

The Skorokhod representation implies that $0\leq X_{t}\leq\Lambda_{t}$ a.s. Consequently, $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{t})\subseteq[0,\Lambda_{t}]$ . Now we establish the inverse inclusion.

#### Lemma 4.8 (Identification of the support).

For every $t>0$ , $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{t})=[0,\Lambda_{t}]$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $t>0$ and $y\in(0,\Lambda_{t})$ . Let $G$ be an arbitrary open neighborhood of $y$ . Choose an open interval $J$ such that $y\in J$ , $\overline{J}\subset G\cap(0,\Lambda_{t})$ . By the continuity of $\Lambda$ , there exists $s<t$ , sufficiently close to $t$ , such that $\inf_{q\in[s,t]}\Lambda_{q}>\sup J$ . By (4.1), $\mathbb{P}[X_{s}>0]>0$ . Applying Lemma 4.4 conditionally on $X_{s}$ gives

$$ \mathbb{P}[X_{t}\in J,\,\tau>t]=\int_{(0,\Lambda_{s}]}\mathbb{P}_{s,x}\big[X_{t}\in J,\ \tau>t\big]\,\mu_{s}(\mathrm{d}x)>0. $$

Therefore, $\mu_{t}(G)\geq\mu_{t}(J)>0$ . Since $G$ is an arbitrary neighborhood of $y$ , we conclude that $(0,\Lambda_{t})\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{t})$ . The support is closed, and $\Lambda_{t}\geq r_{*}>0$ . Hence, it also contains both endpoints, i.e. $[0,\Lambda_{t}]\subset\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{t})$ . Together with the observation made before the lemma, this proves the claim. ∎

The preceding results determine the boundary and the support at every positive time, but they do not yet identify the behavior of the boundary at time zero. We first identify its lower trace using only the stopped path representation and exact balance.

#### Lemma 4.9 (Initial lower trace).

Let $(X,\Lambda)$ be a probabilistic solution with initial law $\mu_{0}$ satisfying Assumption 1.1, and set $a\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ , $b\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ . Then

$$ \liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}=a+b. $$

#### Proof.

Write

$$ q_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t],\quad\underline{\Lambda}_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf_{0<s\leq t}\Lambda_{s},\quad\ell\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\underline{\Lambda}_{t}=\liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}. $$

We first show that $\ell\geq b$ . Since $L_{0}=0$ , the exact balance equation at $t=0$ gives $\mathbb{P}[\tau=0]=0$ . Hence, $q_{t}\downarrow 0$ and

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\alpha q_{t}\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{as }t\downarrow 0. $$

Since $L$ is non-decreasing, it follows that $L_{0+}=0$ almost surely. Moreover, on $\{\tau>0\}$ , one has $L_{t}=K_{t}$ for all sufficiently small $t$ , and therefore $K_{0+}=0$ almost surely. If $\ell<\infty$ , choose $s_{n}\downarrow 0$ such that $\Lambda_{s_{n}}\to\ell$ . Then

$$ 0\leq(X_{0}+B_{s_{n}}-\Lambda_{s_{n}})^{+}\leq K_{s_{n}}\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{almost surely}. $$

Since $B_{s_{n}}\to 0$ , this gives $X_{0}\leq\ell$ almost surely. Thus $b=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}X_{0}\leq\ell$ ; the case $\ell=\infty$ is immediate. Consequently,

$$ \ell=\liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}\geq b. $$

We next determine the small-time logarithmic rate of $q_{t}$ . For every $\varepsilon>0$ ,

$$ p_{\varepsilon}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{0}([a,a+\varepsilon])>0. $$

Since allocation can only decrease the state, the reflection principle gives

$$ q_{t}\geq\mathbb{P}\!\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq t}(X_{0}+B_{s})\leq 0\right]=2\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\mu_{0}(dx)\geq 2p_{\varepsilon}\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\!\left(\frac{a+\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t}}\right). $$

Gaussian tail asymptotics, followed by $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ , yield

$$ \liminf_{t\downarrow 0}t\log q_{t}\geq-\frac{a^{2}}{2}. $$

For the converse estimate, set

$$ \operatorname{osc}_{[0,t]}^{-}B\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq r\leq s\leq t}(B_{r}-B_{s}). $$

Since $\Lambda$ , and hence $K$ , is continuous on $(0,T]$ , default is attained continuously. Thus

$$ X_{0}+B_{\tau}=K_{\tau}\quad\text{on }\{\tau\leq T\}. $$

If $K_{\tau}=0$ , then $B_{\tau}=-X_{0}\leq-a$ . If $K_{\tau}>0$ , choose $r_{n}\in(0,\tau]$ such that

$$ X_{0}+B_{r_{n}}-\Lambda_{r_{n}}\longrightarrow K_{\tau}. $$

Then

$$ B_{r_{n}}-B_{\tau}=X_{0}+B_{r_{n}}-\Lambda_{r_{n}}-K_{\tau}+\Lambda_{r_{n}}\geq\underline{\Lambda}_{t}+o(1), $$

and therefore $\operatorname{osc}_{[0,t]}^{-}B\geq\underline{\Lambda}_{t}$ . Consequently,

$$ q_{t}\leq\mathbb{P}\!\left[-\inf_{0\leq s\leq t}B_{s}\geq a\right]+\mathbb{P}\!\left[\operatorname{osc}_{[0,t]}^{-}B\geq\underline{\Lambda}_{t}\right]. $$

If $M_{s}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq r\leq s}B_{r}$ , then

$$ \operatorname{osc}_{[0,t]}^{-}B=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}(M_{s}-B_{s}). $$

By Lévy’s identity, $(M_{s}-B_{s})_{s\geq 0}$ has the law of reflected Brownian motion $(|B_{s}|)_{s\geq 0}$ . Hence, for every $d>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}[\operatorname{osc}_{[0,t]}^{-}B\geq d]\leq 4\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\!\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{t}}\right). $$

If $a>0$ , fix $d\in(0,a)$ . By (4.13), $\underline{\Lambda}_{t}\geq d$ for all sufficiently small $t$ . Therefore, (4.15) and Gaussian tail asymptotics give

$$ \limsup_{t\downarrow 0}t\log q_{t}\leq-\frac{d^{2}}{2}. $$

Letting $d\uparrow a$ gives the upper bound matching (4.14). If $a=0$ , the matching upper bound follows from $q_{t}\leq 1$ . Thus

$$ \lim_{t\downarrow 0}t\log q_{t}=-\frac{a^{2}}{2}. $$

We next prove

$$ \liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}\geq a+b. $$

If $a=0$ , this follows from (4.13). Suppose $a>0$ . If (4.17) failed, then for some $\delta\in(0,2a)$ and some $t_{n}\downarrow 0$ , $\Lambda_{t_{n}}\leq a+b-\delta$ . Set $\eta\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\delta/4$ and

$$ A_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left\{X_{0}\geq b-\frac{\delta}{4},\quad B_{t_{n}}\geq a-\frac{\delta}{2}\right\}. $$

On $A_{n}$ , $K_{t_{n}}\geq\eta$ . Since $L_{t_{n}}=K_{t_{n}}$ on $\{\tau>t_{n}\}$ , the exact balance equation gives

$$ \alpha q_{t_{n}}\geq\eta\,\mathbb{P}[A_{n}\cap\{\tau>t_{n}\}]\geq\eta\bigl(\mathbb{P}[A_{n}]-q_{t_{n}}\bigr). $$

Equivalently,

$$ q_{t_{n}}\geq\frac{\eta}{\alpha+\eta}\mathbb{P}[A_{n}]. $$

Moreover,

$$ p_{\delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{0}\!\left(\left[b-\frac{\delta}{4},b\right]\right)>0,\quad\mathbb{P}[A_{n}]=p_{\delta}\,\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\!\left(\frac{a-\delta/2}{\sqrt{t_{n}}}\right), $$

where we used the independence of $X_{0}$ and $B$ . Hence

$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}t_{n}\log\mathbb{P}[A_{n}]=-\frac{(a-\delta/2)^{2}}{2}>-\frac{a^{2}}{2}, $$

contradicting (4.16). This proves (4.17).

It remains to prove the reverse inequality. If it failed, then for some $\delta>0$ and all sufficiently small $t$ , $\underline{\Lambda}_{t}\geq a+b+\delta$ . Writing $M_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}B_{s}$ and using $X_{0}\leq b$ almost surely, we obtain

$$ L_{t}\leq K_{t}\leq(M_{t}-a-\delta)^{+}. $$

Exact balance therefore implies

$$ \alpha q_{t}\leq\mathbb{E}[(M_{t}-a-\delta)^{+}]. $$

For every $d>0$ , the reflection principle gives

$$ \mathbb{E}[(M_{t}-d)^{+}]\leq\mathbb{E}[M_{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{M_{t}\geq d\}}]=2\sqrt{t}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{t}}\right). $$

Taking $d=a+\delta$ in (4.18) gives

$$ \limsup_{t\downarrow 0}t\log q_{t}\leq-\frac{(a+\delta)^{2}}{2}, $$

contradicting (4.16). This proves (4.12). ∎

Next, we are going to show that the initial lower trace obtained in Lemma 4.9 actually gives the correct limit of $\Lambda_{t}$ as $t\downarrow 0$ . Towards this goal, we start with proving some technical results about probabilistic solutions.

#### Lemma 4.10 (Protected-path allocation estimate).

Retain the notation

$$ a\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0}),\quad b\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0}),\quad q_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t],\quad h_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{E}[L_{t}]. $$

For every $A\in(a,a+b)$ , there are constants $c_{A}>0$ and $t_{A}>0$ such that, as Stieltjes measures on $(0,t_{A}]$ ,

$$ dq_{t}\geq c_{A}t^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{A^{2}}{2t}\right)dt. $$

Consequently, the exact balance equation gives

$$ dh_{t}\geq\alpha c_{A}t^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{A^{2}}{2t}\right)dt. $$

#### Proof.

Choose $d\in(A,a+b)$ . By Lemma 4.9, after decreasing $t_{A}>0$ if necessary, it holds that $\Lambda_{t}\geq d$ for $t\in(0,t_{A}]$ . Since $a<A$ and $\mu_{0}(\{0\})=0$ , one has $\mu_{0}((0,A))>0$ . We may therefore choose $0<x_{-}<x_{+}<A$ such that, for $I\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=[x_{-},x_{+}]$ , $\mu_{0}(I)>0$ . For Brownian motion $Y^{x}_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=x+B_{t}$ started from $x\in I$ , let $T_{0}$ and $T_{d}$ denote the first hitting times of $0$ and $d$ , respectively. On $\{T_{0}<T_{d},\ T_{0}\leq t_{A}\}$ , the path stays below $d\leq\Lambda_{s}$ for $0<s<T_{0}$ . Hence the regulator vanishes up to $T_{0}$ and $\tau=T_{0}$ . Consequently, for every Borel set $E\subset(0,t_{A}]$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}[\tau\in E]\geq\int_{I}\mathbb{P}_{x}[T_{0}\in E,\ T_{0}<T_{d}]\,\mu_{0}(dx). $$

For $z>0$ , let

$$ f_{z}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{z}{\sqrt{2\pi t^{3}}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{z^{2}}{2t}\right),\quad t>0, $$

be the Brownian first-passage density over distance $z$ . By the strong Markov property at $T_{d}$ , and because the law of $T_{d}$ on $\{T_{d}<T_{0}\}$ is a submeasure of the unrestricted hitting-time law with density $f_{d-x}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{x}[T_{0}\in dt,\ T_{d}<T_{0}]\leq(f_{d-x}*f_{d})(t)\,dt=f_{2d-x}(t)\,dt. $$

It follows that

$$ \frac{\mathbb{P}_{x}[T_{0}\in dt,\ T_{0}<T_{d}]}{dt}\geq f_{x}(t)-f_{2d-x}(t). $$

Moreover, uniformly for $x\in I$ ,

$$ \frac{f_{2d-x}(t)}{f_{x}(t)}=\frac{2d-x}{x}\exp\!\left(-\frac{2d(d-x)}{t}\right)\leq\frac{2d-x_{-}}{x_{-}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{2d(d-x_{+})}{t}\right)\longrightarrow 0 $$

as $t\downarrow 0$ . After decreasing $t_{A}$ once more, we therefore have, for $x\in I$ and $0<t\leq t_{A}$ ,

$$ f_{x}(t)-f_{2d-x}(t)\geq\frac{1}{2}f_{x}(t)\geq\frac{x_{-}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\,t^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{A^{2}}{2t}\right). $$

Combining this estimate with (4.21) proves (4.19), with $c_{A}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{0}(I)x_{-}/(2\sqrt{2\pi})$ . Finally, $h_{t}=\alpha q_{t}$ for every $t$ , and hence $dh=\alpha\,dq$ , proving (4.20). ∎

#### Remark 4.11 (Positive-time support versus the initial trace).

The support identity

$$ \operatorname{supp}(\mu_{t})=[0,\Lambda_{t}] $$

is asserted only for $t>0$ . The initial law may have gaps, and in general $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ need not be an interval of the form $[0,\Lambda_{0}]$ . Lemma 4.9 identifies the lower trace of the boundary. We next prove the matching upper trace from the weak evolution of the ordinary call function; no initial support identity is imposed.

Retain and/or introduce the notations

$$ \mu_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t}),\quad\mu_{t}^{+}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{t}\big|_{(0,\infty)},\quad h_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathbb{E}[L_{t}],\quad m_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}y\,\mu_{0}(dy), $$

and define the ordinary call function

$$ C(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(y-x)^{+}\,\mu_{t}(dy),\quad(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}_{+}. $$

#### Lemma 4.12 (Weak evolution of the ordinary call function).

Under Assumption 1.1, the function $C$ is jointly continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}_{+}$ , and

$$ C(t,0)=m_{0}-h_{t},\quad t\geq 0. $$

Moreover,

$$ \partial_{xx}C(t,\cdot)=\mu_{t}^{+} $$

in the sense of distributions on $(0,\infty)$ . In addition, for every $0\leq s<t\leq T$ and every $\eta\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,\infty))$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle C(t,\cdot)-C(s,\cdot),\eta\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{s}^{t}\langle\mu_{u}^{+},\eta\rangle\,du-\int_{(s,t]}\left(\int_{0}^{\Lambda_{u}}\eta(x)\,dx\right)dh_{u}. $$

Consequently, as locally finite Radon measures on $(0,T)\times(0,\infty)$ ,

$$ \left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)C=-\mathbf{1}_{\{0<x<\Lambda_{t}\}}\,dx\,dh_{t}. $$

Finally, for every $t>0$ ,

$$ C(t,x)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\leq x<\Lambda_{t}. $$

#### Proof.

On $[0,T]$ , the absence of atoms in the law of $\tau$ implies that $h$ is continuous. Since $L$ is non-decreasing, $\mathbb{E}|L_{t}-L_{s}|=|h_{t}-h_{s}|$ . Hence

$$ \mathbb{E}|X_{t}-X_{s}|\leq\mathbb{E}|B_{t\wedge\tau}-B_{s\wedge\tau}|+|h_{t}-h_{s}|\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{as }|t-s|\to 0. $$

Thus $t\mapsto\mu_{t}$ is continuous in $\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ . Since

$$ |C(t,x)-C(s,y)|\leq W_{1}(\mu_{t},\mu_{s})+|x-y|, $$

$C$ is jointly continuous. Since $X_{t}\geq 0$ , optional stopping in the stopped-state identity gives

$$ C(t,0)=\mathbb{E}[X_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}]-\mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=m_{0}-h_{t}, $$

which proves (4.23). For any $C^{2}$ function $\phi$ of at most linear growth with bounded first and second derivatives, Itô’s formula for the stopped reflected process gives

$$ \langle\phi,\mu_{t}\rangle-\langle\phi,\mu_{s}\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{s}^{t}\langle\phi^{\prime\prime},\mu_{u}^{+}\rangle\,du-\int_{(s,t]}\phi^{\prime}(\Lambda_{u})\,dh_{u}. $$

Indeed, before absorption $dL$ is carried by the contact set $\{X=\Lambda\}$ , and its mean Stieltjes measure is $dh$ . The identity first follows for compactly supported smooth $\phi$ and then by a cutoff argument. It is enough here to work on the positive-time interval $[s,t]$ , on which the boundary is bounded. Now, given $\eta\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,\infty))$ , put

$$ K_{\eta}(y)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}(y-x)^{+}\eta(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{y}(y-x)\eta(x)\,dx. $$

Then

$$ K_{\eta}^{\prime}(y)=\int_{0}^{y}\eta(x)\,dx,\quad K_{\eta}^{\prime\prime}(y)=\eta(y),\quad\langle K_{\eta},\mu_{t}\rangle=\langle C(t,\cdot),\eta\rangle. $$

Substituting $K_{\eta}$ into (4.27) proves (4.24). The distributional identity $\partial_{xx}C(t,\cdot)=\mu_{t}^{+}$ follows directly from $\partial_{xx}(y-x)^{+}=\delta_{y}$ on $(0,\infty)$ , and therefore (4.24) is equivalent to (4.25). Finally, $C(t,x)>0$ if and only if $\mu_{t}((x,\infty))>0$ . The support identity $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{t})=[0,\Lambda_{t}]$ for $t>0$ now gives (4.26). ∎

The following positive-set maximum principle is the analytic comparison tool used below. For $Q=(r,S)\times(0,R)$ , write its parabolic boundary as

$$ \partial_{p}Q\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{r\}\times[0,R]\,\cup\,[r,S]\times\{0,R\}. $$

#### Lemma 4.13 (Positive-set parabolic maximum principle).

Let $z\in C(\overline{Q})$ and suppose that $\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)z$ is a locally finite signed Radon measure in $Q$ . Assume that $\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)z\leq 0$ on the open set $\{z>0\}$ in the distributional sense, and that $z\leq 0$ on $\partial_{p}Q$ . Then $z\leq 0$ in $\overline{Q}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\rho>0$ . The parabolic Kato inequality gives

$$ \left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)(z-\rho)^{+}\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{z>\rho\}}\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)z $$

in the sense of distributions. For completeness, the local form of this inequality follows by regularizing $z$ in the interior of $Q$ and applying the chain rule to smooth convex approximations $\beta_{\varepsilon}$ of $r\mapsto r^{+}$ :

$$ \left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)\beta_{\varepsilon}(z)=\beta_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(z)\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)z-\frac{1}{2}\beta_{\varepsilon}^{\prime\prime}(z)|\partial_{x}z|^{2}\leq\beta_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}(z)\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)z. $$

Applying this calculation to $z-\rho$ , passing first through the regularization, and then letting $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ yields (4.28) for measure-valued data. Since $\{z>\rho\}\subset\{z>0\}$ , its right-hand side is non-positive by assumption. Thus $(z-\rho)^{+}$ is a distributional subsolution of the heat equation and has zero parabolic boundary values. The weak parabolic maximum principle gives $(z-\rho)^{+}=0$ . Letting $\rho\downarrow 0$ proves $z\leq 0$ . ∎

The following argument is in the same spirit of Lemma 3.9 as in the discrete-time situation. We present the full proof for completeness.

#### Lemma 4.14 (A probabilistic upper-advance modulus).

Let $0<r<r+\rho\leq T$ . Suppose that, for some $\gamma>0$ ,

$$ dh_{s}\geq\gamma\,ds\quad\text{in the distributional sense on }(r,r+\rho). $$

Then

$$ \Lambda_{r+\rho}-\Lambda_{r}\leq\Omega_{\gamma}(\rho), $$

where

$$ \Omega_{\gamma}(\rho)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf_{\theta>0}\left\{\frac{\log(1+\theta/\gamma)}{2\theta}+\theta\rho\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

Fix $\theta>0$ and set

$$ \beta_{\theta,\gamma}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\log(1+\theta/\gamma)}{2\theta},\quad F_{\theta,\gamma}(y)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\gamma}{2\theta^{2}}\bigl(e^{2\theta y}-1-2\theta y\bigr),\quad y\geq 0. $$

The function $F_{\theta,\gamma}$ is non-negative, non-decreasing, and convex, with

$$ F_{\theta,\gamma}(0)=F_{\theta,\gamma}^{\prime}(0)=0,\quad F_{\theta,\gamma}^{\prime}(\beta_{\theta,\gamma})=1. $$

For $r\leq s\leq r+\rho$ , define

$$ \xi_{s}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\Lambda_{r}+\beta_{\theta,\gamma}+\theta(s-r),\quad W(s,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=F_{\theta,\gamma}\bigl((\xi_{s}-x)^{+}\bigr). $$

Because $F_{\theta,\gamma}(0)=F_{\theta,\gamma}^{\prime}(0)=0$ , differentiation across $x=\xi_{s}$ creates no singular measure. A direct calculation gives

$$ \left(\partial_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)W=-\gamma\mathbf{1}_{\{0<x<\xi_{s}\}}\,dx\,ds. $$

Since $\mu_{r}$ is supported in $[0,\Lambda_{r}]$ , it is clear that $C(r,x)\leq(\Lambda_{r}-x)^{+}$ . For $0\leq x\leq\Lambda_{r}$ , convexity and $F_{\theta,\gamma}^{\prime}(\beta_{\theta,\gamma})=1$ give

$$ W(r,x)=F_{\theta,\gamma}(\beta_{\theta,\gamma}+\Lambda_{r}-x)\geq F_{\theta,\gamma}(\beta_{\theta,\gamma})+\Lambda_{r}-x\geq\Lambda_{r}-x. $$

For $x\geq\Lambda_{r}$ , the inequality $C(r,x)\leq W(r,x)$ is immediate. Moreover, (4.23), the monotonicity of $h$ , and the preceding convexity estimate give, for $r\leq s\leq r+\rho$ ,

$$ C(s,0)=m_{0}-h_{s}\leq m_{0}-h_{r}=C(r,0)\leq\Lambda_{r}\leq W(s,0). $$

Choose $R>\max\left\{\sup_{r\leq s\leq r+\rho}\Lambda_{s},\,\xi_{r+\rho}\right\}$ . Then $C(s,R)=W(s,R)=0$ throughout the interval. Consider

$$ Z\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=C-W,\quad\mathcal{O}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{(s,x)\in(r,r+\rho)\times(0,R)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}Z(s,x)>0\}. $$

Let $\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{O})$ be non-negative and set

$$ G(s)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{0}^{R}\varphi(s,x)\,dx. $$

On $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi)$ , one has $C>0$ , and hence $x<\Lambda_{s}$ by (4.26). Equations (4.25) and (4.32) therefore give

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\left(\partial_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)Z,\varphi\right\rangle \displaystyle=-\int_{(r,r+\rho)}G(s)\,dh_{s}+\gamma\int_{r}^{r+\rho}\int_{0}^{R}\mathbf{1}_{\{x<\xi_{s}\}}\varphi(s,x)\,dx\,ds \displaystyle\leq-\int_{(r,r+\rho)}G(s)\,dh_{s}+\gamma\int_{r}^{r+\rho}G(s)\,ds\leq 0, $$

where the last inequality follows from (4.29). Therefore,

$$ \left(\partial_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)Z\leq 0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathcal{O}). $$

Lemma 4.13 yields $Z\leq 0$ , i.e. $C\leq W$ . At time $r+\rho$ , the barrier vanishes for

$$ x\geq\xi_{r+\rho}=\Lambda_{r}+\beta_{\theta,\gamma}+\theta\rho. $$

Equation (4.26) now gives

$$ \Lambda_{r+\rho}\leq\Lambda_{r}+\beta_{\theta,\gamma}+\theta\rho. $$

Taking the infimum over $\theta>0$ proves (4.30). ∎

#### Proposition 4.15 (Full initial trace of the free boundary).

Let $(X,\Lambda)$ be a probabilistic solution with initial law $\mu_{0}$ satisfying Assumption 1.1, and set $a\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\inf\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ , $b\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ . Then

$$ \lim_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}=a+b. $$

Therefore, the assignment $\Lambda_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=a+b$ extends $\Lambda$ continuously to $[0,T]$ .

#### Proof.

Lemma 4.9 gives

$$ \liminf_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}=a+b. $$

Suppose, towards a contradiction, that $\limsup_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}>a+b$ . Choose $\delta\in(0,b)$ and $t_{n}\downarrow 0$ such that $\Lambda_{t_{n}}\geq a+b+3\delta$ . Choose

$$ A\in(a,a+\delta). $$

By Lemma 4.10, there are $\kappa_{A}>0$ and $t_{A}>0$ such that

$$ dh_{s}\geq\kappa_{A}s^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{A^{2}}{2s}\right)\,ds,\quad 0<s\leq t_{A}. $$

Decrease $t_{A}$ so that $t_{A}<A^{2}/3$ . Then, the density on the right-hand side of (4.36) is increasing on $(0,t_{A}]$ . By (4.34), for all large $n$ we may choose $\sigma_{n}\in(0,t_{n})$ such that $\Lambda_{\sigma_{n}}<a+b+\delta$ . Define

$$ r_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup\{s\in[\sigma_{n},t_{n}]\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\Lambda_{s}\leq a+b+\delta\},\quad\rho_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=t_{n}-r_{n}. $$

Positive-time continuity of $\Lambda$ gives

$$ \Lambda_{r_{n}}=a+b+\delta,\quad\Lambda_{s}>a+b+\delta\quad(r_{n}<s\leq t_{n}),\quad\Lambda_{t_{n}}-\Lambda_{r_{n}}\geq 2\delta. $$

Moreover, $r_{n}\to 0$ and $\rho_{n}\to 0$ . For all large $n$ , (4.36) and the monotonicity of its density imply

$$ dh_{s}\geq\gamma_{n}\,ds\quad\text{on }(r_{n},t_{n}),\quad\gamma_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\kappa_{A}r_{n}^{-3/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{A^{2}}{2r_{n}}\right). $$

We claim that

$$ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\rho_{n}}{r_{n}}>0. $$

Otherwise, after passing to a subsequence,

$$ \varepsilon_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\rho_{n}}{r_{n}}\longrightarrow 0. $$

Apply Lemma 4.14 with

$$ \theta_{n}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(r_{n}\rho_{n})^{-1/2}=(r_{n}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}})^{-1}. $$

Since $\theta_{n}\rho_{n}=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}}$ and

$$ \frac{\theta_{n}}{\gamma_{n}}=\kappa_{A}^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{r_{n}}{\varepsilon_{n}}}\exp\!\left(\frac{A^{2}}{2r_{n}}\right), $$

the elementary inequalities $1+e^{q}u\leq e^{q}(1+u)$ for $q,u\geq 0$ and $\log(1+u)\leq u$ give

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\log(1+\theta_{n}/\gamma_{n})}{2\theta_{n}}\leq\frac{A^{2}}{4}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}}+\frac{r_{n}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}}}{2}\log\left(1+\kappa_{A}^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{r_{n}}{\varepsilon_{n}}}\right)\leq\frac{A^{2}}{4}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}}+\frac{r_{n}^{3/2}}{2\kappa_{A}}. $$

Together with $\theta_{n}\rho_{n}=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}}$ and (4.31), this implies

$$ \Lambda_{t_{n}}-\Lambda_{r_{n}}\leq\left(1+\frac{A^{2}}{4}\right)\sqrt{\varepsilon_{n}}+\frac{r_{n}^{3/2}}{2\kappa_{A}}\longrightarrow 0, $$

contradicting (4.37). Hence, there are $\eta>0$ and $n_{0}$ such that

$$ \rho_{n}\geq\eta r_{n},\quad n\geq n_{0}. $$

Now, choose $\vartheta$ such that

$$ \max\left\{\frac{1}{1+\eta},\frac{A^{2}}{(a+\delta)^{2}}\right\}<\vartheta<1. $$

Then $[\vartheta t_{n},t_{n}]\subset(r_{n},t_{n}]$ . Integrating (4.36) over this interval gives

$$ h_{t_{n}}-h_{\vartheta t_{n}}\geq c_{1}t_{n}^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{A^{2}}{2\vartheta t_{n}}\right) $$

for some $c_{1}>0$ .

For the reverse estimate, let $M_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}B_{s}$ . On the event $\{L_{t_{n}}-L_{\vartheta t_{n}}>0\}$ , the fact that $dL_{u}$ is carried by $\{u<\tau\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}X_{u}=\Lambda_{u}\}$ gives a time $s\in(\vartheta t_{n},t_{n}]$ such that

$$ X_{s}=\Lambda_{s},\quad B_{s}=\Lambda_{s}-X_{0}+L_{s}\geq a+\delta. $$

Moreover, $X_{0}\leq b$ and $\Lambda>0$ imply $L_{t_{n}}\leq K_{t_{n}}\leq b+M_{t_{n}}$ . Thus, pathwise,

$$ L_{t_{n}}-L_{\vartheta t_{n}}\leq(b+M_{t_{n}})\mathbf{1}_{\{M_{t_{n}}\geq a+\delta\}}. $$

The reflection principle and Mills’ inequality therefore give

$$ \displaystyle h_{t_{n}}-h_{\vartheta t_{n}}\leq 2b\,\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\left(\frac{a+\delta}{\sqrt{t_{n}}}\right)+2\sqrt{t_{n}}\,\phi\left(\frac{a+\delta}{\sqrt{t_{n}}}\right)\leq c_{2}\sqrt{t_{n}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(a+\delta)^{2}}{2t_{n}}\right) $$

for some $c_{2}<\infty$ . By (4.38), $A^{2}/\vartheta<(a+\delta)^{2}$ , so (4.39) and (4.40) jointly lead to a contradiction as $n\to\infty$ . We conclude that

$$ \limsup_{t\downarrow 0}\Lambda_{t}\leq a+b. $$

Together with (4.34), this concludes the proof of (4.33). ∎

#### Remark 4.16 (Canonical endpoint).

The full initial trace is obtained without assuming a density trace at the moving upper boundary. The canonical endpoint is

$$ \Lambda_{0}=\inf\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})+\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0}), $$

which need not equal $\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ . No support identity is asserted at time zero: the initial law may be disconnected or singular. The auxiliary convention $\Lambda_{0}^{\Delta}=\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})$ in the discrete scheme in Section 3 may be safely retained, because it is dynamically irrelevant and the compactness argument is deliberately local on $(0,T]$ .

### 4.3 The augmented call-function formulation

The weak evolution of the ordinary call function was established in Lemma 4.12. Adding the cumulative loss $h$ moves its source measure from the continuation region to the coincidence region. We now formulate the resulting obstacle problem without reference to a free boundary.

#### Definition 4.17 (The continuous weak augmented-call class).

Fix an initial law $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ satisfying $\mu_{0}(\{0\})=0$ , and write

$$ m_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu_{0}(dx). $$

We call a pair

$$ H\in C([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}_{+}),\quad h\in C([0,T]) $$

a continuous weak augmented-call solution with initial law $\mu_{0}$ if the following conditions hold:

- 1. The function $h$ is non-decreasing.

- 2. There exists a family $(\mu_{t})_{0\leq t\leq T}\subset\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ , with initial value $\mu_{0}$ , such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ , $\displaystyle H(t,x)-h_{t}$ $\displaystyle=C_{\mu_{t}}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(y-x)^{+}\,\mu_{t}(dy),$ $\displaystyle x\geq 0,$ (4.41) $\displaystyle h_{t}$ $\displaystyle=\alpha\mu_{t}(\{0\}).$

- 3. The conserved first-moment boundary condition holds:

$$ H(t,0)=m_{0},\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

(4.42)

- 4. The distribution

$$ \nu_{H}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)H $$

is a locally finite non-negative Radon measure on $(0,T)\times(0,\infty)$ , and

$$ (H-h)\,\nu_{H}=0. $$

Here, $h$ is identified with the function $(t,x)\mapsto h_{t}$ . Equivalently,

$$ \operatorname{supp}(\nu_{H})\subseteq\{(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}H(t,x)=h_{t}\}. $$

#### Remark 4.18.

Condition 2 gives $h_{0}=0$ . For each $t$ , the measure $\mu_{t}$ is uniquely determined by $(H,h)$ . Indeed,

$$ \partial_{xx}H(t,\cdot)=\mu_{t}\big|_{(0,\infty)},\quad\mu_{t}(\{0\})=\frac{h_{t}}{\alpha}, $$

where the first identity holds in the sense of distributions on $(0,\infty)$ . Moreover, conditions 2–3 imply

$$ \begin{gathered}0\leq h_{t}\leq\alpha,\quad\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}y\,\mu_{t}(dy)=m_{0}-h_{t},\\
0\leq h_{t}\leq H(t,x)\leq m_{0},\quad(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}_{+}.\end{gathered} $$

Furthermore,

$$ \lim_{x\to\infty}H(t,x)=h_{t}. $$

For every $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ , the right derivative of its call function satisfies $\partial_{x}^{+}C_{\mu}(x)=-\mu((x,\infty))$ . Consequently,

$$ \partial_{x}^{+}H(t,0)=-\mu_{t}((0,\infty))=-(1-\mu_{t}(\{0\})),\quad h_{t}=\alpha\bigl(1+\partial_{x}^{+}H(t,0)\bigr). $$

Note that neither a free boundary $\Lambda$ nor a representation of $\nu_{H}$ in terms of such a boundary is included in the definition.

Let $(X,\Lambda)$ be a probabilistic solution under Assumption 1.1, retain the notation $\mu_{t},h_{t}$ , and $C$ from Lemma 4.12, and define

$$ H(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=C(t,x)+h_{t},\quad(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}_{+}. $$

#### Proposition 4.19 (Probabilistic solutions induce weak augmented-call solutions).

The pair $(H,h)$ defined by (4.47) belongs to the continuous weak augmented-call class. More precisely, its obstacle measure admits the sharper representation

$$ \nu_{H}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)H=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq\Lambda_{t}\}}\,dx\,dh_{t} $$

as locally finite Radon measures on $(0,T)\times(0,\infty)$ . In particular,

$$ H\geq h,\quad\nu_{H}\geq 0,\quad(H-h)\nu_{H}=0. $$

Moreover,

$$ \{x\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}H(t,x)=h_{t}\}=[\Lambda_{t},\infty),\quad t>0. $$

#### Proof.

Exact balance shows that $h$ is non-decreasing and that $h_{t}=\alpha\mu_{t}(\{0\})$ . Lemma 4.12 gives the required continuity. The call-function representation holds by construction, while (4.23) gives the boundary condition. Since the distributional time derivative of the spatially constant function $(t,x)\mapsto h_{t}$ is $dx\,dh_{t}$ , equation (4.25) yields

$$ \left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)H=-\mathbf{1}_{\{0<x<\Lambda_{t}\}}\,dx\,dh_{t}+dx\,dh_{t}=\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq\Lambda_{t}\}}\,dx\,dh_{t}, $$

which proves (4.48). This measure is locally finite because, for every $R<\infty$ and $0<s<t<T$ ,

$$ \nu_{H}\bigl((s,t]\times(0,R)\bigr)\leq R(h_{t}-h_{s})\leq R\alpha. $$

Finally, $H-h=C\geq 0$ , and (4.26) gives (4.50). The measure in (4.48) is therefore non-negative and carried by $\{H=h\}$ , proving (4.49) and completing the verification of the definition. ∎

### 4.4 Stability and Uniqueness in the Augmented-Call Topology

We now compare two continuous weak augmented-call solutions with possibly different initial laws. The natural distance must record not only the initial call function, but also its short-time response to absorption at zero.

For $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ , write

$$ C_{\mu}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}(y-x)^{+}\,\mu(dy). $$

Let $(S_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ denote the absorbed Brownian semigroup and define the control-free default curve

$$ q_{\mu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(S_{t}\mu)(\{0\})=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}2\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\mu(dx),\quad t>0, $$

where $\overline{\Phi}_{\mathrm{G}}$ is the standard Gaussian tail. For the fixed horizon $T>0$ , set

$$ d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu,\nu)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|C_{\mu}-C_{\nu}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}+\sup_{0<t\leq T}\bigl|q_{\mu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)-q_{\nu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)\bigr|. $$

#### Theorem 4.20 (Stability of continuous weak augmented-call solutions).

Fix $\alpha>0$ , $T>0$ , and $a_{0}>0$ . For $i=1,2$ , let $\mu_{0}^{i}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ satisfy

$$ \mu_{0}^{i}(\{0\})=0,\quad m_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu_{0}^{i}(dx)\geq\alpha+a_{0},\qquad i=1,2, $$

and let $(H^{i},h^{i})$ be continuous weak augmented-call solutions with initial law $\mu_{0}^{i}$ , $i=1,2$ , respectively. Let $(\mu_{t}^{i})_{0\leq t\leq T}$ be the associated family from Definition 4.17, and write

$$ C^{i}(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H^{i}(t,x)-h_{t}^{i}=C_{\mu_{t}^{i}}(x),\quad q_{t}^{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{t}^{i}(\{0\})=\frac{h_{t}^{i}}{\alpha}. $$

Then there exists $C=C(\alpha,a_{0},T)<\infty$ such that

$$ \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left(\|H^{1}(t,\cdot)-H^{2}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}+|h_{t}^{1}-h_{t}^{2}|\right)\leq C\,d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}). $$

After changing $C$ if necessary,

$$ \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\left(\|C^{1}(t,\cdot)-C^{2}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}+|q_{t}^{1}-q_{t}^{2}|\right)\leq C\,d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}). $$

#### Proof.

Set

$$ \varepsilon\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|C_{\mu_{0}^{1}}-C_{\mu_{0}^{2}}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})},\quad\beta_{T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0<t\leq T}\bigl|q_{\mu_{0}^{1}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)-q_{\mu_{0}^{2}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)\bigr|. $$

Thus $d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2})=\varepsilon+\beta_{T}$ . Set $r\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=a_{0}/2$ .

Step 1: A common continuation strip and obstacle comparison. By (4.44), $0\leq h_{t}^{i}\leq\alpha$ and $C^{i}(t,0)=m_{i}-h_{t}^{i}$ . Since every call function is $1$ -Lipschitz in space,

$$ C^{i}(t,x)\geq C^{i}(t,0)-x=m_{i}-h_{t}^{i}-x\geq a_{0}-x\geq\frac{a_{0}}{2}>0,\quad(t,x)\in[0,T]\times[0,r]. $$

The complementarity condition therefore implies that $\nu_{H^{i}}$ vanishes on $(0,T)\times(0,r)$ , so

$$ \partial_{t}H^{i}=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}H^{i}\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}((0,T)\times(0,r)). $$

Introduce

$$ w\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H^{1}-H^{2},\quad\Delta(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}|h_{s}^{1}-h_{s}^{2}|. $$

We claim that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ ,

$$ \sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq s\leq t\\
x\geq 0\end{subarray}}|H^{1}(s,x)-H^{2}(s,x)|\leq\max\{\varepsilon,\Delta(t)\}. $$

The assertion is immediate for $t=0$ . Fix $t\in(0,T]$ , put $M\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max\{\varepsilon,\Delta(t)\}$ , and, for $\eta>0$ , define

$$ z_{\eta}(s,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H^{1}(s,x)-H^{2}(s,x)-M-\eta(1+x). $$

On the open set $\{z_{\eta}>0\}$ ,

$$ H^{1}>H^{2}+M\geq h^{2}+M\geq h^{1}. $$

Hence $\nu_{H^{1}}$ vanishes there, whereas $\nu_{H^{2}}\geq 0$ , and thus

$$ \left(\partial_{s}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)z_{\eta}=\nu_{H^{1}}-\nu_{H^{2}}=-\nu_{H^{2}}\leq 0\quad\text{on }\{z_{\eta}>0\}. $$

At $s=0$ ,

$$ z_{\eta}(0,x)\leq\varepsilon-M-\eta(1+x)\leq 0, $$

while (4.42) and $|m_{1}-m_{2}|\leq\varepsilon$ give

$$ z_{\eta}(s,0)=m_{1}-m_{2}-M-\eta\leq 0. $$

Finally, (4.44) gives $0\leq H^{i}\leq m_{i}$ . Choose $R_{\eta}<\infty$ so that $\eta(1+R_{\eta})>\max\{m_{1},m_{2}\}$ . Then $z_{\eta}(s,R_{\eta})<0$ for $0\leq s\leq t$ . Applying Lemma 4.13 on $(0,t)\times(0,R_{\eta})$ yields $z_{\eta}\leq 0$ . Letting $\eta\downarrow 0$ and then interchanging the two solutions proves (4.58).

Step 2: Removing the freely evolved initial discrepancy. Let

$$ f\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=C_{\mu_{0}^{1}}-C_{\mu_{0}^{2}},\quad\delta m\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=f(0)=m_{1}-m_{2},\quad v(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(S_{t}f)(x), $$

where the same notation is used for the action of $S_{t}$ on functions. For absorbed Brownian motion $Z$ , symmetry of the killed heat kernel and optional stopping give the put–call identity

$$ \mathbb{E}_{x}[(y-Z_{t})^{+}]=\mathbb{E}_{y}[(Z_{t}-x)^{+}],\quad x,y\geq 0. $$

Fubini’s theorem therefore yields the identity $S_{t}C_{\mu}=C_{S_{t}\mu}$ . Consequently,

$$ v(t,x)=C_{S_{t}\mu_{0}^{1}}(x)-C_{S_{t}\mu_{0}^{2}}(x). $$

Since $f$ is bounded and Lipschitz, $S_{t}f\to f$ uniformly as $t\downarrow 0$ . Moreover, $S_{t}$ is a Markov contraction, and therefore

$$ v(0,\cdot)=f,\quad v(t,0)=\delta m,\quad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|v(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}\leq\varepsilon. $$

Moreover, the call-function derivative formula gives, for $t>0$ ,

$$ \partial_{x}^{+}v(t,0)=q_{\mu_{0}^{1}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)-q_{\mu_{0}^{2}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t). $$

The function $v$ is smooth and satisfies the heat equation $\partial_{t}v=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}v$ on $(0,\infty)\times(0,\infty)$ . Now, set $Y\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=w-v$ on $[0,T]\times[0,r]$ . Equations (4.57) and (4.59) show that

$$ \partial_{t}Y=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}Y\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}((0,T)\times(0,r)),\quad Y(0,\cdot)=0,\quad Y(\cdot,0)=0. $$

Therefore, for $Y$ , the only nonzero parabolic boundary datum is $b(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Y(t,r)$ .

Step 3: The Dirichlet-to-Neumann estimate and boundary feedback. For $k>0$ , set

$$ \lambda_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{k^{2}}{2},\quad\rho_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\alpha\frac{k}{\sinh(kr)},\quad\|g\|_{\lambda,T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}e^{-\lambda t}|g(t)|, $$

and put $\Delta_{\lambda,T}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|h^{1}-h^{2}\|_{\lambda,T}$ . By (4.58),

$$ e^{-\lambda t}|w(t,r)|\leq\max\{\varepsilon,\Delta_{\lambda,T}\},\quad 0\leq t\leq T. $$

Together with (4.59), this gives

$$ \|b\|_{\lambda,T}\leq\varepsilon+\max\{\varepsilon,\Delta_{\lambda,T}\}\leq 2\varepsilon+\Delta_{\lambda,T}. $$

Consider the auxiliary function

$$ \Psi(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\|b\|_{\lambda_{k},T}e^{\lambda_{k}t}\frac{\sinh(kx)}{\sinh(kr)}, $$

which satisfies

$$ \partial_{t}\Psi=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\Psi,\quad\Psi(t,0)=0,\quad\Psi(t,r)\geq|b(t)|. $$

Applying Lemma 4.13 to $Y-\Psi$ and $-Y-\Psi$ gives $|Y|\leq\Psi$ . Since the right derivatives at zero exist by (4.46) and (4.60), dividing by $x$ and letting $x\downarrow 0$ yields

$$ \sup_{0<t\leq T}e^{-\lambda_{k}t}|\partial_{x}^{+}Y(t,0)|\leq\frac{k}{\sinh(kr)}\|b\|_{\lambda_{k},T}. $$

Subtracting the two closure relations (4.46) and using $w=v+Y$ , we obtain, for $t>0$ ,

$$ h_{t}^{1}-h_{t}^{2}=\alpha\bigl(\partial_{x}^{+}v(t,0)+\partial_{x}^{+}Y(t,0)\bigr). $$

Since $h_{0}^{1}=h_{0}^{2}=0$ , equations (4.60), (4.61), and (4.62) give

$$ \Delta_{\lambda_{k},T}\leq\alpha\beta_{T}+\rho_{k}\bigl(2\varepsilon+\Delta_{\lambda_{k},T}\bigr). $$

Consequently, whenever $\rho_{k}<1$ ,

$$ \|h^{1}-h^{2}\|_{\lambda_{k},T}\leq\frac{\alpha\beta_{T}+2\rho_{k}\varepsilon}{1-\rho_{k}}. $$

Because $r>0$ , $\rho_{k}\to 0$ as $k\to\infty$ . Choose $k=k(\alpha,a_{0})$ so that $\rho_{k}\leq 1/2$ . Then

$$ \Delta_{\lambda,T}\leq 2\alpha\beta_{T}+2\varepsilon, $$

and hence

$$ \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}|h_{t}^{1}-h_{t}^{2}|\leq e^{k^{2}T/2}\bigl(2\alpha\beta_{T}+2\varepsilon\bigr). $$

Together with (4.58), this proves (4.53). Finally,

$$ C^{1}-C^{2}=H^{1}-H^{2}-(h^{1}-h^{2}),\quad q^{1}-q^{2}=\frac{h^{1}-h^{2}}{\alpha}, $$

which proves (4.54). ∎

#### Corollary 4.21 (Uniqueness of probabilistic solution).

For every initial law satisfying Assumption 1.1, there is at most one probabilistic free boundary solution in law. More precisely, if $(X^{i},\Lambda^{i})$ , $i=1,2$ , are two probabilistic solutions with initial law $\mu_{0}$ , then $\Lambda^{1}=\Lambda^{2}$ on $[0,T]$ and

$$ \mathcal{L}\bigl((X_{t}^{1})_{0\leq t\leq T}\bigr)=\mathcal{L}\bigl((X_{t}^{2})_{0\leq t\leq T}\bigr). $$

If the two solutions are constructed from the same $X_{0}$ and Brownian motion, then $X^{1}=X^{2}$ almost surely.

#### Proof.

For $i=1,2$ , let $(H^{i},h^{i})$ be the augmented-call pair associated with $(X^{i},\Lambda^{i})$ through (4.47). By Proposition 4.19, both pairs belong to the continuous weak augmented-call class. Set

$$ a_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu_{0}(dx)-\alpha>0. $$

Since $d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0},\mu_{0})=0$ , Theorem 4.20 gives $H^{1}=H^{2},\qquad h^{1}=h^{2}$ . Since $q_{t}^{i}=\frac{h_{t}^{i}}{\alpha}$ and $\quad(\mu_{t}^{i})^{+}=\partial_{xx}H^{i}(t,\cdot)$ in the sense of distributions on $(0,\infty)$ , it follows that $\mu_{t}^{1}=\mu_{t}^{2}$ for every $t\in[0,T]$ . For $t>0$ , (4.50) gives

$$ \Lambda_{t}^{i}=\inf\{x\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}H^{i}(t,x)=h_{t}^{i}\}. $$

Hence $\Lambda_{t}^{1}=\Lambda_{t}^{2}$ for every $t>0$ . By Proposition 4.15, their canonical continuous extensions satisfy

$$ \Lambda_{0}^{1}=\Lambda_{0}^{2}=\inf\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0})+\max\operatorname{supp}(\mu_{0}). $$

Once the deterministic boundary is fixed, the stopped Skorokhod construction makes $X$ a measurable functional of $(X_{0},B)$ . This proves uniqueness of the path law. If the two solutions use the same $X_{0}$ and $B$ , the same representation yields pathwise equality. ∎

#### Remark 4.22 (Comparison with an absorption-flux distance).

For every $x\geq 0$ , the function $y\mapsto(y-x)^{+}$ is $1$ -Lipschitz. Consequently, $\|C_{\mu}-C_{\nu}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}\leq W_{1}(\mu,\nu)$ . Extend the free default curves continuously to time zero by setting $q_{\mu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(0)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu(\{0\})$ and $q_{\nu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(0)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\nu(\{0\})$ . Suppose, in addition, that these extensions are absolutely continuous on $[0,T]$ and write

$$ j_{\mu}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{d}{dt}(S_{t}\mu)(\{0\}),\quad j_{\nu}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{d}{dt}(S_{t}\nu)(\{0\}). $$

Then

$$ q_{\mu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)-q_{\nu}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)=\mu(\{0\})-\nu(\{0\})+\int_{0}^{t}\bigl(j_{\mu}(s)-j_{\nu}(s)\bigr)\,ds, $$

and therefore

$$ \displaystyle d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu,\nu)\leq{} \displaystyle W_{1}(\mu,\nu)+|\mu(\{0\})-\nu(\{0\})|+\int_{0}^{T}|j_{\mu}(t)-j_{\nu}(t)|\,dt. $$

As a result, any topology controlling the Wasserstein distance, the initial absorbed mass, and the $L^{1}$ distance between the free absorption fluxes also controls $d_{T}^{\sharp}$ .

### 4.5 Positive-time classical regularity

We now show that probabilistic solutions actually satisfy the free boundary system (1.1) classically at positive times. Throughout this subsection, let $(X,\Lambda)$ be a probabilistic solution under Assumption 1.1, and retain the notation $\mu_{t}$ , $h_{t}$ , $C$ , and $H$ from Lemma 4.12 and (4.47). Set

$$ r_{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{0}-\alpha>0,\quad\mathcal{D}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}0<t<T,\ 0<x<\Lambda_{t}\}. $$

By Lemma 4.3, $\Lambda_{t}\geq r_{*}$ . We first obtain smoothness of the loss flux at the fixed boundary, then prove a positive density bound near the moving boundary. This bound excludes singular points of the associated parabolic obstacle problem; boundary Harnack estimates then yield smoothness of the moving boundary.

#### Lemma 4.23 (Smooth loss flux and density representation).

The function $h$ belongs to $C^{\infty}((0,T))$ . For every $t\in(0,T)$ ,

$$ \mu_{t}=\frac{h_{t}}{\alpha}\delta_{0}+u(t,x)\mathbf{1}_{\{0<x<\Lambda_{t}\}}\,\mathrm{d}x, $$

where $u=\partial_{xx}H$ is smooth and strictly positive in $\mathcal{D}$ and satisfies $\partial_{t}u=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}u$ there. It is also smooth up to $x=0$ , locally at positive times, with

$$ u(t,0)=0,\quad g(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\dot{h}_{t}=\frac{\alpha}{2}\partial_{x}u(t,0)>0,\quad 0<t<T. $$

Moreover, $C_{x}$ is jointly continuous on $(0,T)\times(0,\infty)$ , $C_{xx}$ and $C_{t}$ are locally bounded there, and

$$ C(t,\Lambda_{t})=C_{x}(t,\Lambda_{t})=0,\qquad 0<t<T. $$

#### Proof.

Equations (4.48) and (4.42) imply

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})(H-m_{0})=0\quad\text{on }(0,T)\times(0,r_{*}),\quad H(t,0)-m_{0}=0. $$

To justify odd reflection, write $w=H-m_{0}$ and note that

$$ |w(t,x)|=|C(t,x)-C(t,0)|\leq x. $$

For a smooth test function $\varphi$ compactly supported in $(0,T)\times(-r_{*},r_{*})$ , put $\psi(t,x)=\varphi(t,x)-\varphi(t,-x)$ for $x>0$ . Test the equation for $w$ against $\chi_{\delta}(x)\psi(t,x)$ , where $\chi_{\delta}$ vanishes for $x\leq\delta$ , equals one for $x\geq 2\delta$ , and has first and second derivatives bounded by constants times $\delta^{-1}$ and $\delta^{-2}$ , respectively. The terms containing $\chi_{\delta}^{\prime}\psi_{x}$ and $\chi_{\delta}^{\prime\prime}\psi$ tend to zero: their integrals are $O(\delta)$ because $|w|\leq x$ and $\psi(t,x)=O(x)$ . Letting $\delta\downarrow 0$ proves that the odd extension of $w$ solves the heat equation distributionally across zero. Interior heat regularity therefore makes $H$ smooth up to $x=0$ , locally at positive times. By (4.46),

$$ h_{t}=\alpha\bigl(1+H_{x}(t,0)\bigr), $$

so $h\in C^{\infty}((0,T))$ .

By Proposition 4.19, $(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})H=0$ in $\mathcal{D}$ . Therefore, $u\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H_{xx}$ is smooth there and satisfies the heat equation. Convexity gives $u\geq 0$ . For every nonempty open interval $J$ compactly contained in $(0,\Lambda_{t})$ , the spatial distributional identity $H_{xx}(t,\cdot)=\mu_{t}^{+}$ and Lemma 4.8 give

$$ \int_{J}u(t,x)\,dx=\mu_{t}(J)>0. $$

If $u$ vanished at an interior point, the strong parabolic minimum principle on a fixed cylinder contained in $\mathcal{D}$ would force it to vanish on a spatial interval at an earlier time, contradicting this identity. Thus, $u>0$ in $\mathcal{D}$ . The odd reflection above makes $u$ odd across zero, so $u(t,0)=0$ . Fix $t_{0}\in(0,T)$ and choose $b\in(0,r_{*})$ and $d>0$ such that $[t_{0}-d,t_{0}+d]\subset(0,T)$ . On the fixed cylinder $(t_{0}-d,t_{0}+d)\times(0,b)$ , $u$ is smooth up to zero, positive in the interior, and zero at $x=0$ . The parabolic Hopf lemma therefore gives $u_{x}(t_{0},0)>0$ . Since $t_{0}$ was arbitrary, differentiation of the closure relation yields

$$ \partial_{x}u(t,0)>0,\quad\dot{h}_{t}=\alpha H_{xt}(t,0)=\frac{\alpha}{2}H_{xxx}(t,0)=\frac{\alpha}{2}\partial_{x}u(t,0). $$

Equation (4.25) now reads

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})C=-g(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{C>0\}}\quad\text{on }(0,T)\times(0,\infty). $$

Its right-hand side is locally bounded, so interior parabolic $L^{p}$ estimates give $C\in W^{2,1}_{p,\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p>1$ . Parabolic Sobolev embedding with $p>3$ , the parabolic dimension being $1+2=3$ , yields joint continuity of $C_{x}$ . Since $C(t,x)=0$ for $x\geq\Lambda_{t}$ , this proves (4.67). For every $a>0$ , the one-sided derivatives of a call function satisfy

$$ C_{x}^{+}(t,a)=-\mu_{t}((a,\infty)),\quad C_{x}^{-}(t,a)=-\mu_{t}([a,\infty)). $$

Their continuity at $a=\Lambda_{t}$ excludes an atom there. The interior density identity, the support identification, and $\mu_{t}(\{0\})=h_{t}/\alpha$ now prove (4.65).

We obtain the bounded-derivative estimate by reducing the equation to one with a constant source. Fix a cylinder compactly contained in $(0,T)\times(0,\infty)$ , set $\Omega_{C}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{C>0\}$ , and define a smooth function $\rho$ on its time interval with $\rho^{\prime}=g-1$ . For $W(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=C(t,x)+\rho(t)$ , equation (4.68) gives

$$ \frac{1}{2}W_{xx}-W_{t}=1\quad\text{a.e. on }\Omega_{C}. $$

On the open set $x>\Lambda_{t}$ , both $C_{xx}$ and $C_{t}$ vanish. The graph $x=\Lambda_{t}$ has two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero by Fubini’s theorem. Hence, almost everywhere on the complementary set,

$$ W_{xx}=0,\qquad W_{t}=g(t)-1, $$

so both derivatives are bounded there. The strong Sobolev regularity of $W$ follows from that of $C$ . After translation and parabolic rescaling, all hypotheses of [16, Theorem 1.1] therefore hold. That theorem requires no sign condition on $W$ and no identification of $\Omega_{C}$ with its nonzero set. It gives $W_{xx},W_{t}\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ , and therefore $C_{xx},C_{t}\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ . In particular, $C$ is locally Lipschitz in time and locally $C^{1,1}$ in space. ∎

#### Lemma 4.24 (Non-degeneracy near the free boundary).

Set $\ell\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=r_{*}/2$ . For every $0<\varepsilon<S<T$ , there exist constants $0<c_{\varepsilon,S}\leq A_{\varepsilon,S}<\infty$ such that

$$ c_{\varepsilon,S}\leq u(t,x)\leq A_{\varepsilon,S},\quad\varepsilon\leq t\leq S,\quad\ell\leq x<\Lambda_{t}. $$

Consequently,

$$ C(t,\Lambda_{t}-z)\geq\frac{c_{\varepsilon,S}}{2}z^{2},\quad\varepsilon\leq t\leq S,\quad 0\leq z\leq\ell. $$

#### Proof.

First, $H$ is non-decreasing in time. Indeed, (4.43) and (4.48) give the non-negative distribution

$$ \partial_{t}H=\frac{1}{2}\mu_{t}^{+}(dx)\,dt+\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq\Lambda_{t}\}}\,dx\,dh_{t}\geq 0. $$

Testing against a non-negative smooth spatial function shows that its integral against $H(t,\cdot)$ is non-decreasing in time. Joint continuity and localization of the spatial test function then give this monotonicity for every fixed $x$ . Choose $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $\delta_{0}>0$ with $S+\delta_{0}<T$ , and set

$$ R>\max_{t\in[s,S+\delta_{0}]}\Lambda_{t},\quad\gamma\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\min_{t\in[s,S+\delta_{0}]}g(t)>0. $$

For $0<\delta<\delta_{0}$ , define on $[s,S]\times[0,R]$

$$ D_{\delta}(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{H(t+\delta,x)-H(t,x)}{\delta}\geq 0. $$

On the coincidence set $C(t,x)=0$ , the inequality $H\geq h$ gives

$$ D_{\delta}(t,x)\geq\frac{h_{t+\delta}-h_{t}}{\delta}\geq\gamma. $$

Globally on the open rectangle, equation (4.48) gives

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})D_{\delta}=\frac{g(t+\delta)\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq\Lambda_{t+\delta}\}}-g(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq\Lambda_{t}\}}}{\delta}. $$

In particular, this right-hand side is bounded for each fixed $\delta$ . Restricted to the open set $C(t,x)>0$ , the second term vanishes, so

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})D_{\delta}(t,x)=\frac{g(t+\delta)}{\delta}\mathbf{1}_{\{x\geq\Lambda_{t+\delta}\}}\geq 0. $$

Let $v$ be the solution to

$$ \begin{cases}(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})v=0,&s<t<S,\quad 0<x<R,\\
v(s,x)=0,&0\leq x\leq R,\\
v(t,0)=0,\quad v(t,R)=\gamma(1-e^{-(t-s)}),&s\leq t\leq S.\end{cases} $$

The maximum principle gives $0\leq v\leq\gamma$ and $v(t,x)>0$ for $t>s$ and $0<x\leq R$ . Set $w_{\delta}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=v-D_{\delta}$ . At the initial time, $w_{\delta}(s,\cdot)\leq 0$ because $D_{\delta}\geq 0$ . At $x=0$ , both terms vanish, while at $x=R$ ,

$$ D_{\delta}(t,R)=\frac{h_{t+\delta}-h_{t}}{\delta}\geq\gamma\geq v(t,R). $$

Thus $w_{\delta}$ is non-positive on the parabolic boundary. Moreover, (4.72) implies

$$ \{v-D_{\delta}>0\}\subseteq\{C>0\}. $$

For each fixed $\delta$ , $w_{\delta}$ has local parabolic Sobolev regularity and $(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})w_{\delta}\in L^{\infty}$ . The Kato inequality and (4.73) therefore give

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})(w_{\delta})^{+}\leq\mathbf{1}_{\{w_{\delta}>0\}}(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})w_{\delta}\leq 0. $$

The weak maximum principle yields $(w_{\delta})^{+}=0$ , hence $D_{\delta}\geq v$ . This comparison uses only bounded right-hand sides. For a fixed $(t,x)\in\mathcal{D}$ , continuity of $\Lambda$ keeps $(t+\delta,x)$ in $\mathcal{D}$ for all sufficiently small $\delta$ . Interior smoothness of $H$ then gives, on letting $\delta\downarrow 0$ ,

$$ u(t,x)=2H_{t}(t,x)\geq 2v(t,x). $$

The minimum of $v$ on $[\varepsilon,S]\times[\ell,R]$ is strictly positive, proving the lower bound in (4.69). For the upper bound, Lemma 4.23 gives a finite essential bound for $C_{xx}$ on the ambient compact rectangle $[\varepsilon,S]\times[\ell,R]$ , which crosses the free boundary. Continuity of $u=C_{xx}$ inside $\mathcal{D}$ upgrades that bound to a pointwise bound there. Finally, (4.65) gives

$$ C(t,\Lambda_{t}-z)=\int_{\Lambda_{t}-z}^{\Lambda_{t}}(y-\Lambda_{t}+z)\,u(t,y)\,dy\geq\frac{c_{\varepsilon,S}}{2}z^{2}, $$

because $z\leq\ell$ and $\Lambda_{t}\geq 2\ell$ . ∎

#### Theorem 4.25 (Positive-time classical regularity).

Under Assumption 1.1, every probabilistic solution satisfies $\Lambda\in C^{\infty}((0,T))$ . The density in (4.65) is smooth up to both spatial boundaries, locally at positive times; or equivalently,

$$ (t,z)\longmapsto u(t,z\Lambda_{t})\quad\text{belongs to }C^{\infty}((0,T)\times[0,1]). $$

The pair $(u,\Lambda)$ satisfies (1.1) classically for $0<t<T$ . In particular,

$$ \displaystyle u(t,0) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle u(t,\Lambda_{t}) \displaystyle=2\dot{h}_{t}=\alpha\partial_{x}u(t,0)>0, \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\partial_{x}u(t,\Lambda_{t}) \displaystyle=-\dot{\Lambda}_{t}\,u(t,\Lambda_{t}), $$

where the traces at $\Lambda_{t}$ are taken from the interior.

#### Proof.

Fix $0<\varepsilon_{0}<\varepsilon<S<S_{0}<T$ , put $\ell=r_{*}/2$ , and let $c,A>0$ be the constants in Lemma 4.24 on $[\varepsilon_{0},S_{0}]$ . We work locally near the graph $\Gamma\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\{(t,\Lambda_{t})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\varepsilon_{0}<t<S_{0}\}$ , away from $x=0$ . By Lemma 4.23, $C\in W^{2,1}_{\infty,\mathrm{loc}}$ , $g=\dot{h}$ is smooth and strictly positive, and (4.68) is the parabolic obstacle equation

$$ C\geq 0,\quad\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)C=-g(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{C>0\}}. $$

Moreover, (4.67) and (4.69) give, for $\varepsilon_{0}\leq t\leq S_{0}$ and $0\leq z\leq\ell$ ,

$$ \frac{c}{2}z^{2}\leq C(t,\Lambda_{t}-z)\leq\frac{A}{2}z^{2},\quad cz\leq-C_{x}(t,\Lambda_{t}-z)\leq Az. $$

Step 1: Every point of $\Gamma$ is regular. Fix $(t_{0},x_{0})\in\Gamma$ and consider the parabolic rescalings

$$ C_{r}(s,y)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=r^{-2}C(t_{0}+r^{2}s,x_{0}+ry). $$

The local bounds on $C_{t}$ and $C_{xx}$ , together with $C(t_{0},x_{0})=C_{x}(t_{0},x_{0})=0$ , give locally uniform bounds

$$ 0\leq C_{r}(s,y)\leq\frac{A}{2}y^{2}+L|s| $$

for some $L<\infty$ , and locally uniform subsequential convergence, including on the time slice $s=0$ . The blow-up classification for the parabolic obstacle problem applies after normalizing the diffusion coefficient and $g(t_{0})$ ; see [22, Theorem 1.2 and equation (1.3)]. In particular, a singular blow-up has the form $P(s,y)=ay^{2}+bs$ for $s\leq 0$ , whereas a degenerate blow-up is zero. However, every blow-up limit $C_{0}$ satisfies

$$ C_{0}(0,y)=0\quad\text{for }y\geq 0,\quad C_{0}(0,y)\geq\frac{c}{2}y^{2}\quad\text{for }y<0. $$

These identities exclude the zero blow-up. They also exclude every singular polynomial: the first forces $a=0$ , contradicting the second. Thus $(t_{0},x_{0})$ is a regular point, with blow-up $g(t_{0})(y_{-})^{2}$ , where $y_{-}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\max\{-y,0\}$ . By [22, Theorem 1.7], $\Gamma$ is locally $C_{p}^{1}$ , where $C_{p}^{\beta}$ denotes parabolic Hölder regularity with time having weight two. In addition, [4, Corollary 6.4] gives

$$ \lim_{\begin{subarray}{c}(t,x)\to(t_{0},\Lambda_{t_{0}})\\
(t,x)\in\mathcal{D}\end{subarray}}C_{t}(t,x)=0. $$

The latter result allows a positive Hölder continuous source depending on both space and time, so its hypotheses hold for $g(t)$ . Consequently, both $C_{t}$ and $C_{x}$ have continuous zero traces on $\Gamma$ . No sign condition on $C_{t}$ is needed.

Step 2: Boundary Harnack and the boundary velocity. Set $p\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=-C_{x}$ and $q\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=C_{t}$ in $\mathcal{D}$ . Differentiating (4.68) in the interior gives

$$ \left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)p=0,\quad\left(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\right)q=-g^{\prime}(t). $$

Both functions vanish continuously on $\Gamma$ and are locally bounded up to it. In a sufficiently small neighborhood of any point of $\Gamma$ , the density lower bound yields

$$ p(t,x)=\int_{x}^{\Lambda_{t}}u(t,y)\,dy\geq c(\Lambda_{t}-x)\geq c\,d_{p}(t,x), $$

where $d_{p}$ is the parabolic distance to the local free boundary. The last inequality follows by using the same-time boundary point $(t,\Lambda_{t})$ . Therefore, [21, Theorem 1.2], applied with its parameter $\varepsilon=1/2$ , gives

$$ R\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{q}{p}=\frac{C_{t}}{-C_{x}}\in C_{p}^{1/2} $$

locally up to $\Gamma$ .

To identify the boundary trace of $R$ without presupposing differentiability of $\Lambda$ , fix a compact time interval $J$ in such a neighborhood. For every sufficiently small $a>0$ , the equation

$$ C(t,\lambda_{a}(t))=a,\qquad t\in J, $$

defines a unique smooth curve in the interior collar. The preceding quadratic bound and the implicit function theorem give

$$ 0\leq\Lambda_{t}-\lambda_{a}(t)\leq\sqrt{2a/c},\quad\lambda_{a}^{\prime}(t)=R(t,\lambda_{a}(t)). $$

Hence, $\lambda_{a}\to\Lambda$ and $\lambda_{a}^{\prime}\to R(\cdot,\Lambda_{\cdot})$ uniformly on $J$ . Passing to the limit in the integral identity for $\lambda_{a}$ proves that $\Lambda\in C^{1}(J)$ and

$$ \dot{\Lambda}_{t}=R(t,\Lambda_{t}), $$

where the right-hand side denotes the interior trace. Since $\Lambda$ is now locally Lipschitz and $R\in C_{p}^{1/2}$ , this trace is $1/4$ -Hölder continuous in time. Therefore, $\Lambda\in C^{1,1/4}_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T))$ .

Step 3: Higher regularity. Suppose inductively that $\Lambda\in C^{k,1/4}_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T))$ for an integer $k\geq 1$ . Then $\Gamma$ is locally $C_{p}^{2k+1/2}$ . The coefficients in the equations for $p,q$ are constant, their sources $0,-g^{\prime}$ are smooth, and the lower bound for $p$ remains valid. Applying [21, Theorem 1.3] with $\beta=2k+1/2$ therefore gives $R\in C_{p}^{2k+1/2}$ locally up to $\Gamma$ . Its trace $t\mapsto R(t,\Lambda_{t})$ belongs to $C^{k,1/4}$ . Indeed, $k$ time derivatives of this composition involve only derivatives of $R$ of parabolic order at most $2k$ and derivatives of $\Lambda$ of order at most $k$ ; the top-order terms are $1/4$ -Hölder continuous along the locally Lipschitz graph. The chain rule at the boundary follows by first working on the interior curves $x=\Lambda_{t}-\eta$ and then letting $\eta\downarrow 0$ . Equation (4.75) now yields $\Lambda\in C^{k+1,1/4}_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,T))$ . Induction proves $\Lambda\in C^{\infty}((0,T))$ .

Step 4: Density regularity and the boundary identities. Near the now smooth moving boundary, $C$ solves the linear equation

$$ C_{t}-\frac{1}{2}C_{xx}=-g(t)\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D},\quad C(t,\Lambda_{t})=0. $$

Local boundary Schauder estimates imply that $C$ , and hence $u=C_{xx}$ , is smooth up to that boundary from the interior. Lemma 4.23 gives smoothness up to $x=0$ , and interior heat regularity covers the region between the two boundary collars. A finite cover on each compact positive-time interval therefore gives

$$ (t,z)\longmapsto u(t,z\Lambda_{t})\in C^{\infty}((0,T)\times[0,1]). $$

Taking the interior trace in (4.68) and using the zero trace of $C_{t}$ gives

$$ u(t,\Lambda_{t})=C_{xx}(t,\Lambda_{t})=2g(t)=\alpha\partial_{x}u(t,0). $$

Differentiating $C_{x}(t,\Lambda_{t})=0$ gives

$$ C_{tx}(t,\Lambda_{t})+\dot{\Lambda}_{t}C_{xx}(t,\Lambda_{t})=0. $$

Since $C_{tx}=\frac{1}{2}C_{xxx}$ in $\mathcal{D}$ , this is the last identity in (4.74). The heat equation for $u$ and its zero trace at $x=0$ were established in Lemma 4.23, completing the proof. ∎

#### Remark 4.26 (Time endpoints).

No classical regularity at $t=0$ is asserted: the initial law in Assumption 1.1 may be singular. The preceding conclusions also hold up to $t=T$ with one-sided time derivatives. Indeed, one may construct a solution from the same initial law on a longer horizon using Section 3. By Corollary 4.21, its restriction agrees with the given solution, including the canonically normalized boundary. The terminal time $T$ is then an interior time for the extended solution.
