### 5.1 Stability of the value function

#### Proposition 5.1 (Stability of the value function).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.20, let $f$ be any payoff allowed in item 2 of Definition 2.1, and let flows $(\mu_{t}^{i})_{t\in[0,T]}$ be corresponding to the unique probabilistic solutions to (1.1) such that

$$ V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}^{i})=\langle f,\mu_{T}^{i}\rangle,\quad i=1,2. $$

Then there exists $C=C(\alpha,a_{0},T)<\infty$ such that

$$ \bigl|V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}^{1})-V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}^{2})\bigr|\leq C\bigl(f(1)-f(0)\bigr)d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}). $$

#### Proof.

Set

$$ d\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}),\quad r\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{a_{0}}{2},\quad w\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H^{1}-H^{2},\quad\delta m\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{1}-m_{2}. $$

Since $|\delta m|\leq d$ , estimate (4.53) gives, after enlarging the constant $C$ if necessary,

$$ \|w-\delta m\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}_{+})}\leq Cd. $$

On the common continuation strip $[0,T]\times[0,r]$ , (4.57) and the identity $H^{i}(t,0)=m_{i}$ show that $z\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=w-\delta m$ solves

$$ \partial_{t}z=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}z\quad\text{on }(0,T)\times(0,r),\quad z(t,0)=0. $$

Odd reflection across $x=0$ , followed by the interior gradient estimate for the heat equation on $[T/2,T)\times[-r/2,r/2]$ , yields

$$ \sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}T/2\leq t<T\\
|x|\leq r/2\end{subarray}}|\partial_{x}z(t,x)|\leq Cd. $$

Consequently,

$$ |z(T,a)|\leq Cda,\quad 0<a\leq\frac{r}{2}. $$

Here, the last estimate is passed from $t<T$ to $T$ by continuity. Moreover,

$$ D_{\mu_{T}^{i}}(a)=m_{i}-H^{i}(T,a), $$

and hence

$$ D_{\mu_{T}^{1}}(a)-D_{\mu_{T}^{2}}(a)=-z(T,a). $$

Combining the local estimate with the global bound on $z$ , and enlarging $C=C(\alpha,a_{0},T)$ once more, gives

$$ \bigl|D_{\mu_{T}^{1}}(a)-D_{\mu_{T}^{2}}(a)\bigr|\leq Cd(a\wedge 1),\quad a>0. $$

Also, (4.54) gives

$$ |q_{T}^{1}-q_{T}^{2}|+|m_{\mu_{T}^{1}}-m_{\mu_{T}^{2}}|\leq Cd. $$

Write the decomposition (2.7) as

$$ f(x)=f(0)+J_{f}\mathbf{1}_{\{x>0\}}+\ell x+\int_{(0,\infty)}(x\wedge a)\,\gamma(da). $$

Then, by Fubini’s theorem,

$$ \langle f,\mu_{T}^{i}\rangle=f(0)+J_{f}(1-q_{T}^{i})+\ell m_{\mu_{T}^{i}}+\int_{(0,\infty)}D_{\mu_{T}^{i}}(a)\,\gamma(da). $$

It follows from (5.2) that

$$ \displaystyle\bigl|V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}^{1})-V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}^{2})\bigr|\leq Cd\left(J_{f}+\ell+\int_{(0,\infty)}(a\wedge 1)\,\gamma(da)\right)=Cd\bigl(f(1)-f(0)\bigr), $$

where the last identity follows by evaluating (2.7) at $x=1$ . ∎

#### Proposition 5.2 (Positive-time stability of the free boundary).

Fix $\alpha>0$ , $T>0$ , and an initial law $\mu_{*}$ satisfying Assumption 1.1. For every $\tau\in(0,T]$ , there exist $\rho,K>0$ , depending only on $\alpha,\mu_{*},\tau,T$ , such that the following holds. If $\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}$ satisfy Assumption 1.1 and

$$ d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{i},\mu_{*})<\rho,\qquad i=1,2, $$

then their corresponding free boundaries satisfy

$$ \sup_{\tau\leq t\leq T}|\Lambda_{t}^{1}-\Lambda_{t}^{2}|\leq Kd_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}). $$

Consequently, if $\mu_{0}^{n},\mu_{0}$ satisfy Assumption 1.1 and $W_{1}(\mu_{0}^{n},\mu_{0})\to 0$ , then the corresponding free boundaries satisfy

$$ \sup_{\tau\leq t\leq T}|\Lambda_{t}^{n}-\Lambda_{t}|\longrightarrow 0\quad\text{for every }\tau\in(0,T]. $$

#### Proof.

We first consider any two initial laws satisfying Assumption 1.1 with a common reserve margin

$$ m_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu_{0}^{i}(dx)\geq\alpha+a_{0},\quad i=1,2, $$

where $a_{0}>0$ . Write

$$ d\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2}),\quad C^{i}(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H^{i}(t,x)-h_{t}^{i},\quad g^{i}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\dot{h}_{t}^{i}. $$

By Lemma 4.23, the functions $g^{i}$ are smooth and strictly positive at positive times. Moreover, (4.68) and (4.26) give

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})C^{i}=-g^{i}(t)\mathbf{1}_{\{C^{i}>0\}},\quad\{x\geq 0\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}C^{i}(t,x)>0\}=[0,\Lambda_{t}^{i}). $$

Regularity at $t=T$ is understood as in Remark 4.26.

Step 1: Stability of the loss flux. Set $r\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=a_{0}/2$ and

$$ w\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=H^{1}-H^{2}-(m_{1}-m_{2}). $$

By (4.57) and (4.42),

$$ (\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})w=0\quad\text{on }(0,T)\times(0,r),\quad w(t,0)=0. $$

Since $|m_{1}-m_{2}|\leq d$ , estimate (4.53) gives

$$ \|w\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T]\times[0,r])}\leq K_{0}d, $$

where $K_{0}$ depends only on $\alpha,a_{0},T$ . Odd reflection across $x=0$ , as in the proof of Lemma 4.23, followed by interior heat estimates yields, for every $s\in(0,T)$ ,

$$ \sup_{s\leq t<T}|\partial_{t}\partial_{x}w(t,0)|\leq K_{s}d, $$

with $K_{s}=K_{s}(\alpha,a_{0},s,T)$ . Differentiating (4.46) gives $g^{1}-g^{2}=\alpha\partial_{t}\partial_{x}w(\cdot,0)$ . Passing to $t=T$ by continuity, we obtain

$$ \sup_{s\leq t\leq T}|g^{1}(t)-g^{2}(t)|\leq K_{s}d. $$

Together with (4.54), this shows that

$$ D_{s}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\leq t\leq T\\
x\geq 0\end{subarray}}|C^{1}(t,x)-C^{2}(t,x)|\leq K_{0}d,\quad B_{s}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{s\leq t\leq T}|g^{1}(t)-g^{2}(t)|\leq K_{s}d. $$

Step 2: A comparison estimate for the support boundaries. Fix $0<s<\theta\leq T$ . For this step, regard the first solution as a reference and abbreviate

$$ (C,g,\Lambda)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(C^{1},g^{1},\Lambda^{1}),\quad(\widetilde{C},\widetilde{g},\widetilde{\Lambda})\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(C^{2},g^{2},\Lambda^{2}). $$

Suppose that, for some $R,\gamma>0$ ,

$$ \Lambda_{t}\leq R,\quad g(t)\geq\gamma,\quad s\leq t\leq T. $$

These bounds are imposed only on the reference solution. Set

$$ a\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{a_{0}}{4},\quad p\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{a_{0}}{2R},\quad Q(t,x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=-C_{x}(t,x)=\mu_{t}^{1}((x,\infty)). $$

The support bound gives $C(t,x)\leq RQ(t,x)$ for $x>0$ . Also, by (4.44) and the spatial $1$ -Lipschitz property of call functions,

$$ Q(t,2a)\geq\frac{C(t,2a)}{R}\geq\frac{a_{0}-2a}{R}=p. $$

Define

$$ \kappa_{s}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{B_{s}+D_{s}/(\theta-s)}{\gamma},\quad\sigma_{s}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{\kappa_{s}R+D_{s}/p}{1-\kappa_{s}}. $$

Assume $D_{s}+B_{s}$ is small enough that

$$ \kappa_{s}<\frac{1}{2},\quad\sigma_{s}<a. $$

For $s\leq t\leq T$ and $x\geq a$ , set

$$ e_{s}(t)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=D_{s}\left(\frac{\theta-t}{\theta-s}\right)^{+}, $$

and introduce the barriers

$$ \displaystyle U_{s}(t,x) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(1-\kappa_{s})C(t,x-\sigma_{s})+e_{s}(t), \displaystyle V_{s}(t,x) \displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=(1+\kappa_{s})C(t,x+\sigma_{s})-e_{s}(t). $$

We claim that

$$ V_{s}\leq\widetilde{C}\leq U_{s}\quad\text{on }[s,T]\times[a,\infty). $$

We first verify the initial and lateral inequalities. Since $Q(t,\cdot)$ is non-increasing,

$$ C(t,x-\sigma_{s})-C(t,x)\geq\sigma_{s}Q(t,x),\quad C(t,x)-C(t,x+\sigma_{s})\geq\sigma_{s}Q(t,x+\sigma_{s}). $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle(1-\kappa_{s})C(t,x-\sigma_{s})-C(t,x) \displaystyle\geq\bigl((1-\kappa_{s})\sigma_{s}-\kappa_{s}R\bigr)Q(t,x)=\frac{D_{s}}{p}Q(t,x)\geq 0, \displaystyle C(t,x)-(1+\kappa_{s})C(t,x+\sigma_{s}) \displaystyle\geq(\sigma_{s}-\kappa_{s}R)Q(t,x+\sigma_{s})\geq 0. $$

Here, the definition of $\sigma_{s}$ also gives $\sigma_{s}-\kappa_{s}R\geq D_{s}/p$ . At $x=a$ , both differences are at least $D_{s}$ , because

$$ Q(t,a)\geq p,\quad Q(t,a+\sigma_{s})\geq Q(t,2a)\geq p. $$

It follows that

$$ V_{s}(t,a)\leq\widetilde{C}(t,a)\leq U_{s}(t,a). $$

At $t=s$ , the required ordering follows from $e_{s}(s)=D_{s}$ and $|\widetilde{C}-C|\leq D_{s}$ .

Next, on the open set $\{\widetilde{C}>U_{s}\}$ , we have $\widetilde{C}>0$ because $U_{s}\geq 0$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})(\widetilde{C}-U_{s}) \displaystyle=-\widetilde{g}+(1-\kappa_{s})g\,\mathbf{1}_{\{C(t,x-\sigma_{s})>0\}}-e_{s}^{\prime} \displaystyle\leq B_{s}-\kappa_{s}\gamma+\frac{D_{s}}{\theta-s}=0. $$

Similarly, on $\{V_{s}>\widetilde{C}\}$ , we have $C(t,x+\sigma_{s})>0$ , so

$$ \displaystyle(\partial_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx})(V_{s}-\widetilde{C}) \displaystyle=-(1+\kappa_{s})g-e_{s}^{\prime}+\widetilde{g}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\widetilde{C}>0\}} \displaystyle\leq B_{s}-\kappa_{s}\gamma+\frac{D_{s}}{\theta-s}=0. $$

These inequalities hold distributionally; the function $e_{s}$ is Lipschitz and satisfies $-e_{s}^{\prime}\leq D_{s}/(\theta-s)$ almost everywhere. Now, choose a finite right endpoint lying beyond both support boundaries and the shifted reference boundary throughout $[s,T]$ . Such an endpoint exists by continuity of the individual boundaries. At this endpoint,

$$ V_{s}=-e_{s}\leq 0=\widetilde{C}\leq e_{s}=U_{s}. $$

Lemma 4.13, applied to $\widetilde{C}-U_{s}$ and $V_{s}-\widetilde{C}$ , proves the claimed comparison. The size of this rectangle does not enter the estimates. For $t\geq\theta$ , we have $e_{s}(t)=0$ , and therefore

$$ (1+\kappa_{s})C(t,x+\sigma_{s})\leq\widetilde{C}(t,x)\leq(1-\kappa_{s})C(t,x-\sigma_{s}). $$

Since $\Lambda_{t}\geq a_{0}=4a$ by Lemma 4.3 and $\sigma_{s}<a$ , identification of the positivity sets gives

$$ \Lambda_{t}-\sigma_{s}\leq\widetilde{\Lambda}_{t}\leq\Lambda_{t}+\sigma_{s},\quad\theta\leq t\leq T. $$

Using $\kappa<1/2$ in (5.5), we conclude that

$$ \sup_{\theta\leq t\leq T}|\widetilde{\Lambda}_{t}-\Lambda_{t}|\leq 2\left[\frac{R}{\gamma}B_{s}+\left(\frac{R}{\gamma(\theta-s)}+\frac{1}{p}\right)D_{s}\right]. $$

Step 3: Uniformity in a neighborhood of the reference law. Let

$$ m_{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\mu_{*}(dx),\quad a_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{m_{*}-\alpha}{2}>0. $$

For every initial law $\nu$ ,

$$ \left|\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}x\,\nu(dx)-m_{*}\right|\leq d_{T}^{\sharp}(\nu,\mu_{*}). $$

Hence, all sufficiently close initial laws have the common reserve margin $a_{0}$ .

Write $(\Lambda^{*},g^{*})$ for the boundary and loss flux associated with $\mu_{*}$ . First apply Step 2 with this solution as reference, taking $s=\tau/4$ and $\theta=\tau/2$ . The reference boundary is bounded on $[\tau/4,T]$ , and the reference flux has a strictly positive minimum there. Step 1 therefore implies, after choosing $\rho>0$ sufficiently small, that

$$ \sup_{\tau/2\leq t\leq T}|\Lambda_{t}^{\nu}-\Lambda_{t}^{*}|\leq K_{*}d_{T}^{\sharp}(\nu,\mu_{*}) $$

whenever $\nu$ satisfies Assumption 1.1 and $d_{T}^{\sharp}(\nu,\mu_{*})<\rho$ . In particular, these boundaries have a common upper bound on $[\tau/2,T]$ .

By (5.4), shrinking $\rho$ further also gives a common strictly positive lower bound for $g^{\nu}$ on $[\tau/2,T]$ . We may now apply Step 2 to any two initial laws in this neighborhood, with $s=\tau/2$ and $\theta=\tau$ . The constants $R,\gamma,a_{0},p$ can be chosen uniformly. Moreover, Step 1 and

$$ d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{0}^{2})\leq d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{1},\mu_{*})+d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{2},\mu_{*})<2\rho $$

ensure $\kappa<1/2$ and $\sigma<a$ after one final reduction of $\rho$ . Estimate (5.7) now proves (5.3).

Step 4: Continuity under Wasserstein convergence. Suppose $W_{1}(\mu_{0}^{n},\mu_{0})\to 0$ . Since

$$ \|C_{\mu_{0}^{n}}-C_{\mu_{0}}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}\leq W_{1}(\mu_{0}^{n},\mu_{0}), $$

it remains to control the free default curves in (4.52). For every $\eta\in(0,T)$ , formula (4.51) gives

$$ \sup_{\eta\leq t\leq T}|q_{\mu_{0}^{n}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)-q_{\mu_{0}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi\eta}}\,W_{1}(\mu_{0}^{n},\mu_{0}). $$

For $0<t\leq\eta$ , monotonicity of the free default curves gives

$$ |q_{\mu_{0}^{n}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)-q_{\mu_{0}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(t)|\leq q_{\mu_{0}^{n}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(\eta)+q_{\mu_{0}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(\eta). $$

Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\eta\downarrow 0$ proves uniform convergence on $(0,T]$ , because $q_{\mu_{0}}^{\mathrm{fr}}(\eta)\to\mu_{0}(\{0\})=0$ . Thus, $d_{T}^{\sharp}(\mu_{0}^{n},\mu_{0})\to 0$ , and the asserted boundary convergence follows from (5.3). ∎

### 5.2 Uniqueness of the optimal control

Throughout this subsection, let Assumption 1.1 hold. Let $(X,\Lambda)$ be the probabilistic solution constructed in Section 3, which is unique by Corollary 4.21, and retain the notations

$$ \mu_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathcal{L}(X_{t}),\quad q_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mu_{t}(\{0\}),\quad h_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\alpha q_{t},\quad D_{t}(a)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=D_{\mu_{t}}(a),\quad m_{0}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{\mu_{0}}. $$

For an arbitrary admissible system $(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{B},\widetilde{L},\widetilde{\tau})\in\mathfrak{A}(\mu_{0})$ , use the analogous notation $\widetilde{\mu}_{t}$ , $\widetilde{q}_{t}$ , $\widetilde{h}_{t}$ , and $\widetilde{D}_{t}$ , and set the difference $d_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=D_{t}-\widetilde{D}_{t}$ .

#### Lemma 5.3 (Dominance and strict propagation).

For every admissible system and every $t\in[0,T]$ ,

$$ \mu_{t}\succsim_{2}\widetilde{\mu}_{t},\quad d_{t}(a)\geq 0\quad(a>0),\quad q_{t}\leq\widetilde{q}_{t}. $$

Moreover, if $0<s<t\leq T$ and $0<r<\inf_{v\in[s,t]}\Lambda_{v}$ , then

$$ d_{t}(a)\geq\int_{0}^{r}p_{r}(t-s,a,y)\,d_{s}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y,\quad 0<a<r, $$

where $p_{r}$ is the transition density of Brownian motion killed upon exiting $(0,r)$ . Consequently, if $d_{s}\not\equiv 0$ on $(0,r)$ , then $d_{t}(a)>0$ for every $a\in(0,r)$ and $\widetilde{q}_{t}>q_{t}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $t>0$ . Applying (3.17) on $[0,t]$ with meshes $\Delta_{k}=t/k$ gives $\mu_{t}^{\Delta_{k}}\succsim_{2}\widetilde{\mu}_{t}$ . The compactness and identification argument in the proof of Theorem 3.1, together with Corollary 4.21, identifies every subsequential cutoff limit with the restriction of $\mu$ to $[0,t]$ . Passing to the limit in the bounded continuous functions $x\mapsto x\wedge a$ and using (2.8) proves (5.8).

For nonnegative $\eta\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,\infty))$ , set

$$ F_{\eta}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}(x\wedge a)\,\eta(a)\,\mathrm{d}a. $$

Extend $\eta$ by zero at $0$ . Then

$$ F_{\eta}^{\prime}(x)=\int_{x}^{\infty}\eta(a)\,da\geq 0,\quad F_{\eta}^{\prime\prime}(x)=-\eta(x). $$

Write $\widetilde{L}^{c}$ for the continuous part of $\widetilde{L}$ . Since $\Delta\widetilde{X}_{z}=-\Delta\widetilde{L}_{z}$ , Itô’s formula with jumps gives, for $0\leq u<v\leq T$ ,

$$ \displaystyle F_{\eta}(\widetilde{X}_{v})-F_{\eta}(\widetilde{X}_{u})={} \displaystyle\int_{u}^{v}F_{\eta}^{\prime}(\widetilde{X}_{z-})\,d\widetilde{B}_{z\wedge\widetilde{\tau}}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{u}^{v}\eta(\widetilde{X}_{z})\,dz-\int_{(u,v]}F_{\eta}^{\prime}(\widetilde{X}_{z})\,d\widetilde{L}_{z}^{c} \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{u<z\leq v}\bigl(F_{\eta}(\widetilde{X}_{z})-F_{\eta}(\widetilde{X}_{z-})\bigr). $$

Here, the jump part of the allocation integral has been combined with Itô’s jump correction, and the survival indicator in the second-order term is omitted because $\eta(0)=0$ . The continuous allocation term is non-positive, and each jump contribution satisfies

$$ F_{\eta}(\widetilde{X}_{z})-F_{\eta}(\widetilde{X}_{z-})=-\int_{\widetilde{X}_{z}}^{\widetilde{X}_{z-}}\left(\int_{y}^{\infty}\eta(a)\,da\right)dy\leq 0. $$

The stochastic integral has mean zero because $F_{\eta}^{\prime}$ is bounded, while the allocation terms are integrable by $\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{L}_{T}]<\infty$ . Taking expectations therefore yields

$$ \langle\widetilde{D}_{v}-\widetilde{D}_{u},\eta\rangle\leq-\frac{1}{2}\int_{u}^{v}\langle\widetilde{\mu}_{z}^{+},\eta\rangle\,dz=\frac{1}{2}\int_{u}^{v}\langle\widetilde{D}_{z},\eta^{\prime\prime}\rangle\,dz, $$

where $\widetilde{\mu}_{z}^{+}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\widetilde{\mu}_{z}|_{(0,\infty)}$ . The last equality follows from $\partial_{aa}\widetilde{D}_{z}=-\widetilde{\mu}_{z}^{+}$ in the sense of distributions on $(0,\infty)$ . Hence, $\widetilde{D}$ is a distributional subsolution of the heat equation. Since $D=m_{0}-H$ , equation (4.48) shows that $D$ solves the heat equation on $(s,t)\times(0,r)$ . Therefore, $d$ is a nonnegative distributional supersolution there, with $d_{v}(0)=0$ .

We justify comparison despite possible jumps of the competitor. The uniform spatial Lipschitz bound and càdlàgness of $\widetilde{X}$ imply that $d$ is càdlàg with values in $C([0,r])$ . Moreover, $d_{v}\geq d_{v-}$ , since $D$ is continuous and $\widetilde{X}$ has only downward jumps. Define

$$ d^{\varepsilon}(v,a)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int_{0}^{\varepsilon}d(v+\theta,a)\,d\theta,\quad s\leq v\leq t-\varepsilon. $$

These are continuous supersolutions with nonnegative lateral boundary values. Let $P^{r}$ be the killed semigroup with kernel $p_{r}$ , and choose $\chi_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}((0,r))$ with $0\leq\chi_{n}\uparrow 1$ on $(0,r)$ . Applying Lemma 4.13 to

$$ P^{r}_{v-s}\bigl(\chi_{n}d^{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot)\bigr)(a)-d^{\varepsilon}(v,a) $$

gives $d^{\varepsilon}(v,\cdot)\geq P^{r}_{v-s}(\chi_{n}d^{\varepsilon}(s,\cdot))$ . Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$ proves the comparison for $v<t$ . Letting $v\uparrow t$ and using $d_{t}\geq d_{t-}$ proves (5.9), including at $t=T$ .

Strict positivity in $(0,r)$ follows from positivity of $p_{r}$ . Finally,

$$ \lim_{a\downarrow 0}\frac{d_{t}(a)}{a}=\widetilde{q}_{t}-q_{t}. $$

Dividing (5.9) by $a$ , applying Fatou’s lemma, and using $\partial_{a}p_{r}(t-s,0+,y)>0$ for $0<y<r$ gives the strict default inequality $q_{t}<\widetilde{q}_{t}$ . ∎

#### Theorem 5.4 (Uniqueness of the continuous-time optimal control).

Let $f$ be any non-constant payoff allowed in item 2 of Definition 2.1. If $(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{B},\widetilde{L},\widetilde{\tau})\in\mathfrak{A}(\mu_{0})$ satisfies

$$ \mathbb{E}[f(\widetilde{X}_{T})]=V_{f}(0,\mu_{0}), $$

then

$$ \widetilde{\mu}_{t}=\mu_{t},\qquad 0\leq t\leq T, $$

and, almost surely,

$$ \widetilde{L}_{t}=\sup_{0<s\leq t\wedge\widetilde{\tau}}\bigl(\widetilde{X}_{0}+\widetilde{B}_{s}-\Lambda_{s}\bigr)^{+},\quad 0\leq t\leq T, $$

where the supremum is understood to be zero at $t=0$ . Consequently, the optimal flow and the joint law of the optimal state and control are unique. Optimal systems driven by the same initial state and Brownian motion are indistinguishable.

#### Proof.

Equality of the flow before $T$ . Suppose that $\widetilde{\mu}_{s}\neq\mu_{s}$ for some $s\in(0,T)$ . Then $d_{s}(a_{0})>0$ for some $a_{0}\in(0,\Lambda_{s})$ . Indeed, if $d_{s}=0$ on this interval, taking the right derivative at zero gives $\widetilde{q}_{s}=q_{s}$ , and (3.8) gives equality of the means. Letting $a\uparrow\Lambda_{s}$ then shows that $\widetilde{\mu}_{s}$ has no mass above $\Lambda_{s}$ . The truncated moments therefore agree at every strike, which identifies the two laws.

By the continuity of $\Lambda$ , choose $u\in(s,T)$ and $r>a_{0}$ with $r<\inf_{v\in[s,u]}\Lambda_{v}$ . Lemma 5.3 gives $\widetilde{q}_{u}>q_{u}$ , so $d_{u}$ is strictly positive near zero. Set $r_{*}\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=m_{0}-\alpha>0$ . Since $\Lambda\geq r_{*}$ by Lemma 4.3, applying the same lemma on $(0,r_{*}/2)$ gives $\widetilde{q}_{v}>q_{v}$ , $u<v\leq T$ . In fact, it must hold that

$$ d_{T}(a)>0,\quad a>0. $$

For $a<\Lambda_{T}$ , choose $v\in(u,T)$ close enough to $T$ and $r>a$ with $r<\inf_{w\in[v,T]}\Lambda_{w}$ . The strict default gap at $v$ makes $d_{v}$ positive near zero, so (5.9) yields (5.12). For $a\geq\Lambda_{T}$ , the support identity and resource conservation give

$$ D_{T}(a)=m_{\mu_{T}},\quad\widetilde{D}_{T}(a)\leq m_{\widetilde{\mu}_{T}}=m_{\mu_{T}}-\alpha(\widetilde{q}_{T}-q_{T})<m_{\mu_{T}}. $$

Using the coefficients $J_{f},\ell,\gamma$ from (2.7), we obtain

$$ \langle f,\mu_{T}\rangle-\langle f,\widetilde{\mu}_{T}\rangle=(J_{f}+\alpha\ell)(\widetilde{q}_{T}-q_{T})+\int_{(0,\infty)}d_{T}(a)\,\gamma(da)>0. $$

The inequality is strict because $f$ is nonconstant. This contradicts the assumed optimality of $(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{B},\widetilde{L},\widetilde{\tau})$ , so $\widetilde{\mu}_{t}=\mu_{t}$ for all $t<T$ .

Equality at $T$ . Càdlàgness of $\widetilde{X}$ and continuity of the canonical flow give $\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{X}_{T-})=\mu_{T}$ . Condition (3.4), together with absorption at default, implies $\{\widetilde{X}_{T}=0\}=\{\widetilde{X}_{T-}=0\}$ almost surely, and hence $\widetilde{q}_{T}=q_{T}$ . Exact balance and continuity of $h$ now give

$$ \mathbb{E}[\Delta\widetilde{L}_{T}]=\widetilde{h}_{T}-\widetilde{h}_{T-}=h_{T}-h_{T-}=0. $$

Therefore, $\widetilde{X}_{T}=\widetilde{X}_{T-}$ almost surely, proving (5.10).

Identification of the control. By Lemma 4.8, flow identification, and Proposition 4.15, a countable dense set of times containing $T$ , together with càdlàgness of $\widetilde{X}$ and continuity of $\Lambda$ , gives

$$ 0\leq\widetilde{X}_{t}\leq\Lambda_{t}\quad(0\leq t\leq T),\quad\widetilde{X}_{t-}\leq\Lambda_{t}\quad(0<t\leq T) $$

simultaneously almost surely. In particular, both systems are bounded by $M\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\sup_{[0,T]}\Lambda<\infty$ .

Itô’s formula for $x^{2}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{X}_{T}^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{X}_{0}^{2}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}(1-q_{t})\,dt-2\mathbb{E}\!\int_{(0,T]}\widetilde{X}_{t-}\,d\widetilde{L}_{t}+\mathbb{E}\!\sum_{0<t\leq T}(\Delta\widetilde{L}_{t})^{2}, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[X_{T}^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[X_{0}^{2}] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}(1-q_{t})\,dt-2\int_{(0,T]}\Lambda_{t}\,dh_{t}, $$

where the second identity uses continuity of the canonical regulator and its boundary-contact property. All terms are integrable because $\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{L}_{T}]<\infty$ and $\sum(\Delta\widetilde{L}_{t})^{2}\leq M\widetilde{L}_{T}$ . Since the marginal laws agree and $\mathbb{E}[d\widetilde{L}_{t}]=dh_{t}$ , subtraction yields

$$ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{(0,T]}(\Lambda_{t}-\widetilde{X}_{t-})\,d\widetilde{L}_{t}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{0<t\leq T}(\Delta\widetilde{L}_{t})^{2}\right]=0. $$

Both terms are non-negative. Hence $\widetilde{L}$ is continuous and increases only on $\{\widetilde{X}=\Lambda\}$ . Together with $\widetilde{L}_{0}=0$ and stopping at default, these are the stopped upper Skorokhod conditions, proving (5.11). The resulting state and control are measurable functionals of $(\widetilde{X}_{0},\widetilde{B})$ , which proves the remaining uniqueness assertions. ∎

## 6 Potential Extensions and Further Directions

The cutoff principle rests on two structural properties: conservation of total resources and preservation of increasing-concave order by the uncontrolled dynamics. These properties suggest extensions beyond the present specification. We describe three directions, distinguishing adaptations of the discrete comparison argument from questions requiring further analysis.

#### Nonlinear cumulative losses.

The balance constraint can be replaced by

$$ \mathbb{E}[L_{t}]=\Gamma(q_{t}),\quad q_{t}=\mathbb{P}[\tau\leq t], $$

where $\Gamma(0)=0$ , $\Gamma$ is smooth, and $0<g_{-}\leq\Gamma^{\prime}\leq g_{+}<\infty$ on $[0,1]$ . For example, $\Gamma(q)=\alpha q+\beta q^{2}$ , with $\beta\geq 0$ , allows the loss generated by an additional default to increase with cumulative defaults. Assuming $m_{0}>\Gamma(1)$ , the conserved resource is $m_{\mu}+\Gamma(q_{\mu})$ , and the discrete allocation budget becomes $\Gamma(q_{S_{\Delta}\mu})-\Gamma(q_{\mu})$ . With these substitutions, the truncated-moment comparison and backward induction still give cutoff optimality for the same payoff class; convexity of $\Gamma$ is unnecessary. For a classical reflected limit, the balance condition would read

$$ u(t,\Lambda_{t})=\Gamma^{\prime}(q_{t})u_{x}(t,0). $$

The initial mean condition retains a positive resource margin, while the derivative bounds make allocation budgets comparable to default increments. These conditions provide a concrete route to adapting the compactness and boundary estimates, although the continuous-time extension remains to be proved.

#### State-dependent volatility.

Another extension replaces Brownian motion by the driftless diffusion $\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\sigma(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}B_{t}-\mathrm{d}L_{t}$ before absorption, with a common coefficient $\sigma\in C_{b}^{\infty}([0,\infty))$ satisfying $0<\underline{\sigma}\leq\sigma\leq\overline{\sigma}$ . The absorbed uncontrolled diffusion preserves the mean and increasing-concave order, so the discrete cutoff comparison remains applicable. The call-function formulation also retains a local parabolic structure: writing $H(t,x)=\mathbb{E}[(X_{t}-x)^{+}]+\alpha q_{t}$ , a smooth reflected candidate satisfies

$$ H_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}(x)H_{xx},\qquad\sigma^{2}(\Lambda_{t})u(t,\Lambda_{t})=\alpha\,\partial_{x}(\sigma^{2}u)(t,0). $$

The first identity holds inside the continuation region; the second couples the reflection rate to the default flux. Establishing the continuous limit and its regularity would require variable-coefficient counterparts of the heat-kernel and free boundary estimates used here.

#### Finite populations.

For $N$ banks driven by independent Brownian motions, a natural particle approximation allocates each default loss $\alpha$ by capping the surviving capitals. Its feasibility can be controlled through the empirical resource $R_{t}^{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{i}X_{t}^{i,N}+\alpha q_{t}^{N}$ , where $q_{t}^{N}$ is the default fraction. Stop the system at $\eta_{N}=\inf\{t\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}R_{t}^{N}\leq\alpha\}$ . Before this time all allocations are feasible, and the stopped resource is a continuous martingale with quadratic variation at most $t/N$ . For $\delta>0$ , the condition $R_{0}^{N}\geq\alpha+\delta$ almost surely therefore implies $\mathbb{P}(\eta_{N}\leq T)\leq T/(N\delta^{2})$ . This vanishing probability provides a starting point for connecting the finite system to the optimal mean-field flow. Empirical convergence, identification of the limiting allocation boundary, and asymptotic optimality remain separate questions requiring additional estimates.

## Appendix A Appendix

### Stochastic dominance

#### Lemma A.1 (Decomposition of second-order dominance).

Let $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ . Suppose that $\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ . Then there exists $\eta\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ such that $\eta\succsim_{1}\nu$ and that $\eta$ dominates $\mu$ in convex order: for every convex function $\psi\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ for which the integrals are well-defined,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\psi\,\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\psi\,\mathrm{d}\eta. $$

#### Proof.

The supermartingale-coupling characterization is [24, Theorem 4.A.5]. It states that the assumption $\mu\succsim_{2}\nu$ is equivalent to the existence of random variables $X$ and $Y$ , defined on a common probability space, such that

$$ \displaystyle X\sim\nu,\quad Y\sim\mu,\quad\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\leq Y\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Since $\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ , we may take $X,Y\geq 0$ almost surely. Define $d(Y)\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=Y-\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]$ . Then $d(Y)\geq 0$ almost surely. Now set $Z\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=X+d(Y)$ and define $\eta\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}=\mathrm{Law}(Z)$ . Since $X\geq 0$ and $d(Y)\geq 0$ almost surely, we have $Z\geq 0$ a.s. Thus $\eta\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ . Moreover, since $X$ and $Y$ have finite first moments and $0\leq d(Y)\leq Y+\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]$ , we also have $\mathbb{E}[Z]<\infty$ . As $d(Y)\geq 0$ a.s., it is immediate that $\eta=\mathrm{Law}(Z)\succsim_{1}\mathrm{Law}(X)=\nu$ . It remains to prove the convex-order relation. By construction,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Y]=\mathbb{E}[X+d(Y)\mid Y]=\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]+d(Y)=\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]+Y-\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=Y. $$

Thus, $(Y,Z)$ is a martingale coupling from $\mu$ to $\eta$ . Hence, for every convex function $\psi\mathrel{\mathop{\ordinarycolon}}\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ for which the integrals are well-defined, Jensen’s inequality gives

$$ \displaystyle\psi(Y)=\psi\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Y]\bigr)\leq\mathbb{E}[\psi(Z)\mid Y]. $$

Taking expectations, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\psi(x)\,\mu(dx)=\mathbb{E}[\psi(Y)]\leq\mathbb{E}[\psi(Z)]=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\psi(x)\,\eta(dx). $$

This is precisely the asserted convex-order relation. Together with $\eta\succsim_{1}\nu$ , it proves the claim. ∎
